UNIT.subject: General Science
UNIT.content:
• Absorption of Water and Mineral Salts
• Translocation
• Factors affecting transpiration
• Importance of transpiration
UNIT.learningOutcomes:
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) describe absorption of water and mineral salts in plants,
b) explain translocation in plants,
c) investigate factors affecting transpiration in plants,
d) describe the significance of transpiration in sustainability of plant life,
e) appreciate the role of transport in plants.
UNIT.coreCompetencies:
• Citizenship: as the learner sensitises the community on the importance of watering and manuring plants to sustain plant growth.
• Learning to learn: as the learner reflects on experiments on factors affecting transpiration in plants.
UNIT.values:
• Unity: as the learner engages in assigned roles while working with others in the process of investigation of factors affecting transpiration.
• Patriotism: as the learner sensitises the community on the importance of watering and manuring plants to sustain plant growth.
UNIT.sep:
• Planning and Carrying Out Investigations: as the learner designs and conducts experiments to investigate factors affecting transpiration in plants (e.g., leaf area, wind, humidity, light intensity).
• Analysing and Interpreting Data: as the learner records, compares, and draws conclusions from transpiration experiment results across different environmental conditions.
• Constructing Explanations: as the learner uses evidence from absorption and translocation experiments to explain how water and mineral salts move through a plant.
• Obtaining, Evaluating, and Communicating Information: as the learner uses digital devices and print media to research adhesive and cohesive forces involved in transport, then shares findings with peers.
UNIT.pcis:
• Safety and security: as the learner observes safety precautions while carrying out experiments in groups to investigate factors affecting transpiration in plants.
• Environmental issues: as the learner creates awareness in the community on the use of fertilisers (Di-ammonium Phosphate, Calcium Ammonium Nitrate, Urea) in boosting crop production.
UNIT.careers:
• Agriculture / Agronomy: understanding water and mineral salt absorption directly informs irrigation scheduling, fertiliser application, and crop management on Kenyan farms in areas like the Rift Valley and Kericho.
• Botany / Plant Science: knowledge of translocation and transpiration underpins plant physiology research and breeding programmes at institutions such as KALRO (Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organisation).
• Environmental Science: understanding transpiration and water loss links to watershed management, agroforestry, and conservation of water catchment areas around Mt. Kenya and the Mau Forest.
• Horticulture / Floriculture: flower and vegetable export farms around Naivasha require precise knowledge of plant water transport to maintain produce quality for international markets.
• Biomedical / Pharmaceutical Science: principles of transport across membranes underpin drug delivery and IV fluid therapy studied in nursing and medical training.
UNIT.focus: This unit centres on how plants absorb, move, and lose water and dissolved substances — processes critical to crop survival across Kenya's diverse agro-ecological zones. Learners investigate absorption of water and mineral salts through roots, translocation of organic and inorganic solutes through the phloem and xylem, and the environmental factors that drive or limit transpiration. The unit builds from observable phenomena on a school farm or garden toward molecular-level explanations of cohesion-tension and source-to-sink transport, equipping learners to make evidence-based decisions about watering and fertilising crops in their local communities.
UNIT.phenomenon: A freshly uprooted maize seedling from the school garden in Kisumu is placed with its roots in a beaker of water coloured with red food dye. After 30 minutes, when the stem is cut cross-sectionally, vivid red rings appear in the woody tissue — but the rest of the stem remains white. At the same time, a leafy branch of a succulent plant (e.g., a bean or sweet potato cutting) sealed in a clear polythene bag left in the afternoon sun shows a film of water droplets forming on the inside of the bag within minutes, even though no liquid water was added to the bag. Both observations are puzzling: How does coloured water travel upward against gravity through only certain channels in the stem? And where does all that water vapour inside the bag actually come from — and why does the plant seem to be "losing" water even when it needs it to survive?
UNIT.supportingPhenomena:
• A freshly cut celery stalk placed in coloured water overnight reveals dyed streaks running up through the outer ring of the stalk, making the vascular bundles visible to the naked eye — raising the question of what structures are responsible and how water climbs so high.
• A potted bean plant (common in Kenyan school gardens) left unwatered for two days wilts dramatically; when watered, it recovers within hours — demonstrating that water transport is directly linked to plant structural support (turgor), not just nutrition.
• A banana farmer in the Rift Valley applies Di-ammonium Phosphate (DAP) fertiliser to the soil, and within days the leaves become noticeably greener and more turgid — prompting questions about how dissolved mineral salts reach leaves from soil, and what happens if too much fertiliser is applied.
• On a hot, dry afternoon in Nairobi, the soil under a shady tree feels noticeably cooler and slightly moist compared to bare soil nearby — suggesting that the tree is releasing water vapour through its leaves, with implications for local microclimate and water cycling.
UNIT.drivingQuestion:
DRIVING QUESTION: How does a maize plant in a Kenyan farm move water and nutrients from the soil all the way to its topmost leaves — and what happens to that water in the end?

KICD KEY INQUIRY QUESTION:
1. Why is transport in plants important?
UNIT.storylineThread:
Lesson 1 — PREDICT | Anchoring Phenomenon Introduction: Students observe the dyed-water maize seedling and the sweating polythene-bag demonstrations. Working in pairs, they sketch where they think the red dye will appear in a cross-section and predict where the water droplets in the bag come from. Predictions are posted on the Driving Question Board (DQB). Teacher introduces the driving question and records all student wonder questions. [SEP: Asking Questions]

Lesson 2 — OBSERVE | Structures for Absorption: Learners observe prepared slides or photomicrographs of root hair cells and cross-sections of roots and stems. They identify xylem and phloem using labelled diagrams and digital images. Teacher demonstrates the adhesive and cohesive forces using a capillary tube in water. Students record observations and revisit their Lesson 1 predictions. [SEP: Obtaining and Evaluating Information; Constructing Explanations]

Lesson 3 — EXPLAIN | Absorption of Water and Mineral Salts: Guided discussion on osmosis, active transport, and the root pressure mechanism. Students use print/digital media to research how mineral salts (e.g., DAP — Di-ammonium Phosphate) enter root hair cells and are carried upward. Kenyan context: link to fertiliser use on maize and sukuma wiki farms. Students update the DQB with new explanations. [SEP: Constructing Explanations]

Lesson 4 — OBSERVE & EXPLAIN | Translocation: Learners carry out or observe a demonstration experiment on translocation (e.g., ring-barking/girdling a soft stem, or observing phloem exudate from a cut surface). They discuss the source-to-sink model of phloem transport and compare xylem vs. phloem function using a two-column chart. Peers share findings in plenary. DQB updated with translocation evidence. [SEP: Analysing and Interpreting Data; Constructing Explanations]

Lesson 5 — OBSERVE | Transpiration Experiment Setup: Groups design and set up experiments to investigate factors affecting transpiration — varying one factor each: (a) leaf surface area covered with petroleum jelly, (b) fan creating wind, (c) polythene bag enclosure raising humidity, (d) varying light intensity. Each group states a hypothesis, identifies variables, and records initial measurements. Safety precautions reviewed. [SEP: Planning and Carrying Out Investigations]

Lesson 6 — OBSERVE & ANALYSE | Transpiration Data Collection and Analysis: Groups collect final transpiration measurements, record data in tables, and draw bar/line graphs. Class data is pooled on the board; groups compare results and identify patterns. Teacher facilitates sensemaking: why does wind increase transpiration? How does humidity affect the rate? Link back to the polythene-bag phenomenon from Lesson 1. [SEP: Analysing and Interpreting Data; Obtaining, Evaluating, and Communicating Information]

Lesson 7 — EXPLAIN | Importance of Transpiration and Community Application: Whole-class discussion on the significance of transpiration: cooling of leaves, creation of the transpiration pull (cohesion-tension theory), and mineral salt distribution. Students research and discuss the environmental importance of transpiration for local water cycling (e.g., Mau Forest catchment). Community action component: students draft a short awareness message for farmers on proper watering, manuring, and responsible fertiliser use (DAP, CAN, Urea). DQB revisited and updated. [SEP: Constructing Explanations; Obtaining, Evaluating, and Communicating Information]

Lesson 8 — MODEL BUILDING & DQB CLOSURE | Cumulative Model Revision and Assessment: Students individually revise their Lesson 1 sketches into a complete annotated diagram showing the full journey of a water molecule from soil → root hair → xylem → leaf → stomata → atmosphere, annotating each step with the mechanism (osmosis, cohesion-tension, transpiration pull, active transport for minerals). Groups present their models; peers provide feedback. DQB is reviewed: which questions are now answered? Which remain open? Teacher administers a short performance task (explain why a wilting tomato plant in Mombasa's coastal heat recovers after watering at dusk). [SEP: Developing and Using Models; Constructing Explanations]

LESSONS.title: Anchoring Phenomenon: The Travelling Red Dye & The Sweating Bag

slo.purpose: To launch the sub-strand by anchoring learners in two vivid, puzzling observations — dyed water moving upward through specific channels in a maize stem, and water vapour forming inside a sealed polythene bag around a leafy cutting — so that learners generate genuine questions that will drive the entire Transport in Plants inquiry.
slo.knowledge: Learners will know that (1) water and mineral salts enter plants through roots and move upward through specific vascular tissue, and (2) plants release water vapour through their leaves even when no liquid water is visibly present on them.
slo.skills: Learners will be able to: (a) make and record evidence-based predictions using labelled diagrams; (b) ask testable questions about an observed phenomenon (SEP: Asking Questions); (c) record initial ideas on a Driving Question Board (DQB).
slo.attitudes: Learners appreciate that careful observation of everyday Kenyan farm plants can reveal deep scientific puzzles worth investigating, and develop curiosity and open-mindedness towards unexpected results.
slo.keyInquiry: Why is transport in plants important?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 1 opens the storyline. Learners encounter both dimensions of the driving question simultaneously — upward movement of water through hidden channels (translocation/xylem) and the mysterious loss of water from leaves (transpiration) — without yet receiving any explanation. Their unanswered questions and prediction diagrams seed the DQB and create the intellectual need that will be resolved across subsequent lessons.
slo.safetyNotes: Red food dye is non-toxic but can stain clothing — learners should wear aprons or old clothes. Warn learners not to taste any coloured water. When cutting stems cross-sectionally, the teacher (or a designated learner under close supervision) should use the razor blade on a cutting board away from fingers. Polythene bags should not be placed over faces. Dispose of dyed water responsibly — do not pour into the school garden.

LESSONS.overview: Learners gather around two teacher-led demonstrations: (1) a freshly uprooted maize seedling from the school garden, its roots submerged in water coloured with red food dye, and (2) a leafy sweet potato or bean cutting sealed inside a clear polythene bag placed in a sunny spot. Before any explanation is given, learners individually sketch cross-sections of the maize stem to predict where the red dye will appear, and they predict the origin of the water droplets forming on the inside of the polythene bag. Pairs share predictions, then predictions are posted on the newly created Driving Question Board. The teacher introduces the formal driving question and harvests all learner wonder-questions onto the DQB. No answers are given in this lesson — the goal is to open productive uncertainty. The lesson uses SEP: Asking Questions throughout.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners are shown the two set-up demonstrations BEFORE any results are visible (the dyed-water maize seedling has been soaking for only 5 minutes at this point; the polythene bag has just been sealed around the cutting and placed in sunlight). Working individually for 3 minutes, each learner draws a blank circle (representing a cross-section of the maize stem) in their exercise books and shades in where they predict the red dye will appear after 30 minutes. They also write one sentence answering: 'Where do you think the water droplets inside the polythene bag come from?' Learners then compare their prediction diagrams with a partner (Think-Pair) for 2 minutes, noting agreements and disagreements.
framework.teacherMoves:
1. Hold up the maize seedling (roots in the beaker of red water) and the sealed polythene bag side by side. Say exactly: 'I uprooted this maize plant from our school garden here in Kisumu this morning. I have put its roots in coloured water. I have sealed this sweet potato cutting in a clear bag and placed it in the sun. Do NOT tell me what will happen — I want YOUR ideas first.' 
2. Distribute blank cross-section circle templates (pre-drawn on paper) OR instruct learners to draw a 5 cm circle in their books. Say: 'In this circle, shade the area where you think the red colour will appear when I cut the stem across. There is no wrong answer right now.' 
3. Allow 3 minutes of silent individual thinking. WAIT TIME: do not speak or prompt during these 3 minutes. 
4. Say: 'Now turn to your partner. Compare your diagrams. Agree on one shared prediction and be ready to explain your reasoning.' Allow 2 minutes. 
5. Cold-call exactly 4 pairs (select pairs with visibly different predictions). Ask each pair: 'Show us your diagram and tell us — WHY did you shade that part?' After each response, say: 'Interesting. Hold that thought.' Do NOT confirm or correct. 
6. For the polythene bag: cold-call 3 individual learners. Ask: 'Amina — where do you think that water vapour is coming from?' WAIT 12 seconds after asking before accepting any answer.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: THINK-PAIR-SHARE WITH PREDICTION DIAGRAMS — Learners externalise their mental models by drawing before they have data. This reveals prior conceptions (e.g., 'the whole stem will turn red' vs. 'only the outer ring') and creates a personal stake in finding out whether they were right. The diagram format makes abstract internal anatomy concrete and comparable.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Every learner has a shaded cross-section diagram and a written sentence in their book before pairs share. Teacher scans books during the pair-share to identify: (a) learners who shade the entire circle (no prior knowledge of vascular tissue), (b) learners who shade a ring or spots (partial prior knowledge), (c) learners who draw dots or a central column (alternative conceptions). Teacher mentally notes 2–3 learners from group (a) to revisit in Lesson 3 (Explain phase on xylem).

framework.learnerExperience: After approximately 25 minutes of lesson time have elapsed (the maize seedling has been soaking for ~30 minutes total including setup time before class), the teacher performs the cross-sectional cut live in front of the class. Learners observe the vivid red rings appearing only in the woody vascular tissue. They record what they see in a labelled diagram, writing at least two observations (e.g., 'The red colour appears only in small dots/rings, not in the whole stem' and 'The outer green part and the central pith stayed white'). Simultaneously, learners observe water droplets that have formed on the inside of the polythene bag around the sweet potato or bean cutting. Learners record two observations about the bag ('Droplets formed on the inside surface of the bag' and 'The leaves look the same — no visible water on the outside of the leaves'). Learners annotate their original prediction diagrams with a different-coloured pen to show what they actually observed.
framework.teacherMoves:
1. Build anticipation: 'It has now been about 30 minutes. Let us see what happened.' Carry the maize seedling to the cutting board at the front. Say: 'Watch carefully — I will cut across the stem here' (indicate a point about 5 cm above the roots). Make a clean cross-sectional cut with a sharp razor blade on the cutting board. Hold the cut surface up so all learners can see the red rings. 
2. Say: 'Write down exactly what you see. Not what you think — what you SEE.' Allow 90 seconds of silent recording. 
3. Walk the cut stem around to at least 3 learner pairs for close-up observation. Say: 'Look at the pattern. Can you see any difference between the red parts and the white parts?' WAIT 10 seconds. 
4. Hold up the polythene bag. Say: 'Now look at this bag. I sealed a sweet potato cutting inside it 30 minutes ago. No liquid water was added. What do you observe?' Cold-call 3 learners. After each: 'Write that observation down.' 
5. Instruct: 'Go back to your prediction diagram. Using a RED pen or pencil, draw what you actually observed. Then put a tick if your prediction was right, or a cross if it was different — and write one word describing how you feel about the difference.' 
6. Ask the class: 'How many of you predicted exactly where the red appeared?' (Show of hands — count aloud.) 'How many were surprised?' (Count aloud.) Record counts on the board: e.g., 'Predicted correctly: 4 | Surprised: 28'. Leave these numbers on the board for the DQB phase.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: ANNOTATED OBSERVATION DIAGRAMS WITH PREDICTION COMPARISON — By drawing what they predicted AND then annotating with what they observed using a contrasting colour, learners perform a cognitive comparison that highlights the gap between their prior model and the evidence. The surprise data (only 4 correct out of 32) becomes a shared class experience that motivates explanation-seeking.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Learner books show two layers of annotation — original prediction (one colour) and observed result (contrasting colour/pen). Teacher checks that observations are descriptive, not explanatory (e.g., 'red rings in the woody dots' is acceptable; 'because water went up the xylem' is premature — teacher gently redirects: 'That is an explanation — for now, just tell me what you see'). At least 80% of learners should have two distinct observation statements recorded before the class moves on.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners attempt to construct initial explanations using only the evidence they have just observed — no textbook input yet. In groups of four, learners answer two questions written on the board: (Q1) 'Why do you think the red dye appeared ONLY in those specific parts of the stem — and not everywhere?' (Q2) 'If no liquid water was added to the bag, where could the water vapour have come from?' Groups have 5 minutes to discuss and write a group explanation (2–3 sentences per question) on a strip of manila paper or in their books. Groups share one idea each in a whole-class share-out. Teacher scribes key words from each group on the board under two columns: 'Maize Stem — Dye Ideas' and 'Bag — Water Vapour Ideas'. Teacher does NOT evaluate or correct any idea at this stage.
framework.teacherMoves:
1. Write the two questions on the board in large print before the group work begins. Read them aloud. Say: 'You do not need to know the correct science answer yet. I want YOUR best explanation based only on what you just observed. Use your diagrams as evidence.' 
2. Circulate during the 5 minutes of group work. Listen to group discussions. Prompt quieter groups: 'What did you notice about WHERE the red rings were? Does that give you a clue?' WAIT 12 seconds after each prompt before speaking again. 
3. After 5 minutes, call the class to attention. Take exactly one idea from each of the 6–8 groups (no repeats — if a group has the same idea as a previous group, say 'You agree with Group 3 — noted. Does your group have a different idea?'). 
4. Scribe their exact words — do not paraphrase or correct. Underline key terms learners use (e.g., 'tubes', 'pipes', 'channels', 'skin of the leaf', 'breathing'). 
5. When all groups have shared, step back and say: 'Look at this board. We have several different ideas. They cannot all be right — but they might all point at something true. The experiments in the next few lessons will help us figure out which ideas hold up.' 
6. Say: 'I want to add one word to our vocabulary today — not to explain yet, but so we have a name for the question.' Write 'TRANSPORT IN PLANTS' on the board. 'This sub-strand is about exactly these two mysteries.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: COLLABORATIVE EVIDENCE-BASED ARGUMENTATION (Initial) — Groups are required to ground their explanations in the specific observations they recorded (the diagram evidence), not in recalled knowledge. By scribing all ideas without evaluation, the teacher creates a 'public record of current thinking' that the class will return to and revise across the sub-strand — making learning visible as a process of refinement rather than a single transfer of correct information.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Each group has written at least 2–3 sentences that reference specific observations (e.g., 'We think there are special tubes because the red only went to the dots, not the white parts'). Teacher listens for learners who invoke osmosis, capillary action, or evaporation by name — these learners have relevant prior knowledge and can be paired as peer resources in later lessons. Teacher notes on a class list any groups producing only one-word answers ('pipes') with no reasoning — these groups will receive a sentence-starter scaffold in Lesson 2.

framework.learnerExperience: The class creates its first Driving Question Board together. The teacher reads the formal driving question aloud: 'How does a maize plant on a Kenyan farm move water and nutrients from the soil all the way to its topmost leaves — and what happens to that water in the end?' Each learner writes ONE question of their own — something they genuinely want to know after today's observations — on a sticky note or small piece of paper. Questions are posted on the DQB (a large sheet of manila paper or a section of the classroom wall). The teacher groups the posted questions into clusters in real time: questions about HOW water moves up, questions about WHERE it goes, questions about WHY the plant does this, and questions about WHAT the coloured parts were. The DQB stays on the wall for the entire sub-strand.
framework.teacherMoves:
1. Unroll the large manila paper DQB and fix it to the wall. Write the driving question at the top in large bold letters. Say: 'This is our Driving Question Board. Everything we learn in this sub-strand will help us answer this one big question.' 
2. Hand each learner a sticky note or a small cut piece of paper. Say: 'Write ONE question — your most burning question from what you saw today. It must be a question you genuinely do not know the answer to. Write your name on the back.' Allow 2 minutes of silent writing. 
3. Learners come up row by row to post their questions. As they post, teacher reads each question aloud and asks: 'Should this go near the HOW water moves cluster, or the WHY cluster, or somewhere else?' Let the class decide placement. 
4. After all questions are posted, step back and say: 'Count with me — how many questions have we just created?' Count aloud together. 'All of these are worth investigating. By the end of this sub-strand, we will be able to answer every single one of them.' 
5. Point to specific questions and say: 'This question — Wanjiku's question about why the dye only went to some parts — we will specifically come back to in Lesson 2. This one about the bag — Otieno's question — we tackle in Lesson 4 on transpiration.' 
6. Take a photograph of the DQB (if a phone or tablet is available) for the ARES platform record. Say: 'We will add to this board every lesson. Do not give me the answers yet — let the experiments do that.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: DRIVING QUESTION BOARD — The DQB externalises the class's collective curiosity and creates a living document of the inquiry. By physically mapping questions to future lessons, the teacher makes the sub-strand structure transparent and gives learners agency over the direction of learning. Returning to the DQB each lesson to tick off answered questions reinforces the cumulative, evidence-building nature of scientific inquiry (SEP: Asking Questions).
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Every learner has posted at least one question. Teacher reviews question quality after class — questions should be investigable (e.g., 'What are those dot-shaped parts in the stem?') rather than purely factual-recall ('What is xylem?'). Any learner who writes only a factual-recall question receives a verbal prompt in the next lesson: 'Your question asks for a name — can you turn it into a HOW or WHY question?' Teacher records the total number of questions and their cluster distribution as a baseline measure of prior curiosity and conceptual gaps.

framework.learnerExperience: As the final activity, each learner draws an 'Initial Model' in their exercise book — a simple diagram of a maize plant showing: (a) the roots in the soil near Lake Victoria's shore or a Kisumu farm, (b) the stem, and (c) the leaves at the top. On this diagram, learners draw arrows to show their CURRENT best idea of how water moves from the soil to the topmost leaf, and where they think water 'ends up'. Learners also label anything they are uncertain about with a '?' symbol. These models are NOT collected or corrected — they are dated and kept in the learner's own book to be revised in every subsequent lesson as understanding grows.
framework.teacherMoves:
1. Say: 'Before we finish today, I want you to draw your first model. A model in science is not a perfect picture — it is your current best thinking, shown as a diagram.' 
2. Draw a simple outline of a maize plant on the board (roots, stem, 3–4 leaves). Say: 'Draw something like this in your book. Now add arrows showing where you think water goes. Use a '?' anywhere you are not sure.' 
3. Allow 4 minutes of silent individual drawing. Do not assist — say: 'I want YOUR thinking, not mine.' 
4. Ask 2 learners (cold-call — choose one high-confidence and one quieter learner) to briefly describe their model to the class without showing it: 'Kamau, tell us — where did you draw your arrows going, and why?' WAIT 10 seconds. After Kamau: 'Fatuma, is your model similar or different? What is one thing you marked with a question mark?' 
5. Say: 'Put today's date next to your model and write the words INITIAL MODEL underneath. We will come back to this diagram in every lesson and add to it or change it. By Lesson 5, this same page will look very different — and that change IS the learning.' 
6. Close the lesson: 'Today you observed something that has puzzled scientists for centuries. You made predictions, you observed real evidence, you shared ideas, and you asked great questions. You did exactly what scientists do. Next lesson, we go into the laboratory to find out what those ring-shaped structures in the maize stem actually are.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: CUMULATIVE INITIAL MODEL — By building a personal model on Day 1 before any instruction, learners commit their prior conceptions to paper in a revisable form. The explicit instruction to mark uncertainties with '?' normalises not-knowing as a productive scientific state. Dating the model creates a longitudinal record of conceptual change that learners can celebrate at the sub-strand's end — making the growth of understanding visible and personally meaningful.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Every learner's book has a dated diagram with at least one arrow showing water movement and at least one '?' label. Teacher circulates and notes: (a) learners who draw water moving in a continuous loop (evaporation from leaves → rain → soil → roots → leaves) — these learners have an intuitive sense of the water cycle and will find transpiration meaningful in Lesson 4; (b) learners who draw water moving only to the roots (no upward movement) — these learners need the Lesson 2 xylem evidence most urgently; (c) learners with no arrows at all — teacher writes a brief encouraging note in their book: 'Your question mark shows great scientific honesty. Lesson 2 will give you your first clue.'

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider the following questions: (1) How many learners posted investigable HOW/WHY questions on the DQB versus simple factual-recall questions? If more than 40% posted recall questions, open Lesson 2 with a 5-minute DQB question-refinement activity. (2) Were learners genuinely surprised by the location of the red dye, or did several predict vascular rings correctly? If prior knowledge is higher than expected, increase the complexity of the Lesson 2 observation task. (3) Did any learner connect the polythene bag observation to the concept of sweating or breathing in animals? Note these learners — their analogy can be used in the Lesson 4 transpiration discussion. (4) Was the razor-blade cutting demonstration safe and clearly visible to all learners? If learners at the back could not see the cross-section, plan to prepare 3–4 pre-cut stem sections for Lesson 2 so every pair can examine one up close. (5) Review the DQB question clusters — if no learner asked a question about the white (phloem) tissue or about nutrients (as distinct from water), introduce a teacher-planted question card on the DQB: 'What about the white parts of the stem — do they do anything?' to seed the translocation discussion in Lesson 3.

LESSONS.title: Structures for Absorption: Root Hair Cells, Xylem & Phloem, and Capillary Forces

slo.purpose: Learners gather direct observational evidence — from photomicrographs of root hair cells and stem cross-sections, and from a live capillary-tube demonstration — to identify the specific structures and physical forces responsible for water movement in a maize plant, directly revisiting their Lesson 1 predictions.
slo.knowledge: Learners describe the structure and function of root hair cells; identify xylem and phloem in root and stem cross-section diagrams and photomicrographs; and explain how adhesive and cohesive forces drive water movement through narrow tubes against gravity.
slo.skills: Obtaining and Evaluating Information (SEP): learners examine labelled photomicrographs and diagrams to identify xylem and phloem. Constructing Explanations (SEP): learners connect capillary-rise evidence to the red-dye observation from the phenomenon. Learners also practise scientific drawing of cell structures with accurate labels.
slo.attitudes: Learners appreciate that careful structural observation — as practised by Kenyan agricultural scientists studying crop water-use efficiency — is the foundation for explaining how transport works, and develop curiosity about how invisible physical forces do biological work.
slo.keyInquiry: Why is transport in plants important?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lesson 1, learners recorded predictions about how coloured water travels upward through a maize stem and where the water vapour in the sealed polythene bag comes from. In this OBSERVE lesson, learners gather the structural and physical evidence needed to evaluate those predictions: they see which tissue the red dye actually stains (xylem), understand why xylem tubes are arranged in rings, and watch water climb unaided in a capillary tube — setting the stage for Lesson 3's mechanistic explanation of the cohesion-tension theory.
slo.safetyNotes: Food dye solutions are non-toxic but can stain clothing — learners should wear aprons or old clothes. Glass capillary tubes are fragile; handle with care and place in the foam holder provided. Do not touch cut stem surfaces with bare hands if thorns or sharp pith edges are present. Dispose of used dye solution as directed by the teacher. No open flames in this lesson.

LESSONS.overview: Learners begin by revisiting their Lesson 1 prediction cards about the maize-stem red-dye and polythene-bag phenomena. The teacher then guides three sequential evidence-gathering activities: (1) structured observation of photomicrographs of root hair cells and root/stem cross-sections to identify and label xylem and phloem; (2) a live teacher demonstration of capillary rise using glass tubes of different diameters in water coloured with food dye, drawing the explicit parallel to the narrow xylem vessels seen in the cross-sections; and (3) a gallery walk in which pairs examine six large labelled diagrams posted around the classroom and complete an observation recording sheet. The lesson closes with a whole-class evidence-consolidation discussion in which learners annotate their Lesson 1 prediction cards with new observational evidence, preparing the class Driving Question Board for Lesson 3.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners retrieve their Lesson 1 prediction cards (or exercise-book predictions) about: (a) which part of the maize stem the red dye travelled through, and (b) where the water vapour in the sealed polythene bag came from. Working in pairs for 3 minutes, they re-read their prediction and write one sentence beginning: 'I still think… / I am now less sure about… because…'. Three pairs are cold-called to share aloud. Learners then silently examine the phenomenon photograph on the board — the cross-sectional cut of the red-stained maize stem — for 60 seconds before the teacher poses the focus question.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the phenomenon photo on the projector or a large printed poster (A2 minimum). Say exactly: 'Look at this cut maize stem from our Kisumu school garden. The red rings appeared only in one type of tissue. Before we find out which tissue, re-read your Lesson 1 prediction card. You have 3 minutes with your partner — go.' [Allow 3 minutes.] Cold-call 3 pairs using the name-stick method. After each response, say: 'Thank you — hold that thought. We are going to gather evidence today that will help you decide whether to keep or revise that prediction.' Post the focus question on the board: 'What structures inside a maize stem carry water upward — and what physical forces make that possible?' Allow 10 seconds of silent reading (WAIT TIME).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction Revisitation — by explicitly returning to prior predictions before new input, learners activate relevant prior knowledge and create a cognitive 'gap' (Bransford, 2000) that motivates observation. Connecting to the phenomenon anchors the new vocabulary (xylem, phloem, cohesion, adhesion) to a concrete, visible image rather than an abstract definition.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher listens to the 3 cold-called pairs' responses and mentally notes: Do learners name a specific tissue (e.g., 'the outer ring', 'the coloured part'), or do they use vague language ('it just goes up')? This indicates depth of prior structural understanding. Teacher uses this to calibrate how much scaffolding to provide during Activity 1.

framework.learnerExperience:
ACTIVITY A — Photomicrograph Analysis (20 min): Each pair receives Handout 2A, which contains: (i) a labelled photomicrograph of a root hair cell (showing the elongated hair, thin cell wall, large vacuole, and absence of chloroplasts); (ii) a transverse section (TS) of a root showing the epidermis, cortex, endodermis, and vascular bundle with xylem and phloem clearly stained; (iii) a TS of a maize stem showing the scattered vascular bundles with xylem (large, thin-walled vessels stained red) and phloem (smaller, dense cells). Learners complete a structured observation table: Structure → What I see → Likely function (my best guess). They also make a scientific drawing of the root TS, labelling at least 4 structures.

ACTIVITY B — Capillary Tube Demonstration (15 min): Teacher performs a live demonstration at the front. Three glass capillary tubes of different diameters (wide ~3 mm, medium ~1 mm, narrow ~0.3 mm) are held vertically in a beaker of water coloured red with food dye — the same dye used in the phenomenon. Learners observe and record: (a) the height water rises in each tube; (b) the shape of the meniscus; (c) which tube's water rises highest. Learners record observations on Handout 2B.

ACTIVITY C — Gallery Walk (10 min): Six A2 diagrams are posted around the room: (1) Root hair cell 3D diagram; (2) Root TS with xylem/phloem labelled; (3) Stem TS of maize; (4) Stem TS of bean; (5) Diagram of cohesion (water molecule chain); (6) Diagram of adhesion (water clinging to glass/cell wall). Pairs spend ~90 seconds at each station, writing one observation and one question on a sticky note left at each poster.
framework.teacherMoves:
ACTIVITY A: Distribute Handout 2A. Say: 'You have 20 minutes. Work in pairs. First, read the labels silently — 2 minutes. Then complete the observation table. Then make your scientific drawing. I will circulate. If you are unsure of a label, write your best guess and put a question mark.' Circulate; at 8 minutes, pause the class and cold-call one pair to describe what they see in the xylem vessels vs phloem cells: 'Amina and Brian — describe the xylem to us in your own words. What do you notice about the size and colour of these cells?' [WAIT TIME: 12 seconds.] After their response, add: 'Notice the xylem vessels are large and hollow — they are dead cells. We will come back to why that matters.'

ACTIVITY B: Before starting, say: 'Watch carefully. I am using the same red food dye we placed the maize seedling roots in. What do you predict will happen — write one sentence NOW.' [30-second writing pause.] Slowly lower all three tubes simultaneously into the beaker. Say nothing for 45 seconds — allow learners to observe in silence. Then ask: 'What do you notice? Tell your partner — 30 seconds.' Cold-call 2 pairs. Write their exact words on the board. Then ask: 'Which tube reminds you most of the xylem vessels you just drew?' [WAIT TIME: 15 seconds.] Cold-call 1 learner.

ACTIVITY C: Assign roles — one partner is the 'Recorder', the other is the 'Reader'. Set a timer. Say: 'One observation, one question — sticky note at each poster. Move when the timer beeps. Go.' Circulate and read sticky notes; mentally note any misconceptions (e.g., confusing xylem with phloem, or thinking water is 'pumped' by the roots like a heart).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured Observation with Scaffolded Recording (Observation Table + Scientific Drawing) — the three-column table (Structure / What I see / Likely function) separates raw observation from interpretation, preventing premature closure. The scientific drawing forces learners to attend to spatial relationships (e.g., xylem position relative to phloem) rather than passively viewing. The capillary demonstration provides a physical analogue for the abstract concept of capillary rise, making the invisible mechanism in xylem vessels visible and measurable. The gallery walk with sticky-note questions externalises thinking and generates authentic questions for the Driving Question Board.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher checks observation tables during circulation — specific indicator: learners should correctly identify xylem as large, hollow, and red-stained (or otherwise prominent) in at least 2 of the 3 diagrams. Teacher checks scientific drawings for presence of at least 4 correct labels. During the capillary demo, teacher listens for the key observation: 'the narrowest tube has the highest water.' Sticky notes from the gallery walk are collected and sorted — teacher uses these to identify the 2–3 most prevalent misconceptions to address in the Explain phase (Lesson 3).

framework.learnerExperience: Learners participate in a whole-class 'Connect the Evidence' discussion. The teacher uses a split board: on the left, the phenomenon image (red-stained maize stem TS); on the right, the evidence gathered today. Learners are asked to draw explicit connections: 'Which structure in your photomicrograph matches the red-stained ring in the phenomenon?' and 'How does the capillary demonstration help explain how water gets to the top of a 2-metre maize plant in a Rift Valley farm?' Learners then write a 3-sentence 'evidence statement' in their science journals: 'Today I observed… This evidence suggests… One thing I am still unsure about is…'
framework.teacherMoves: Draw a T-chart on the board: left column 'Phenomenon — what we saw', right column 'Today's evidence — what it tells us'. Say: 'Let's build this together. What did we observe in the phenomenon? Chiamaka?' [WAIT TIME: 10 seconds.] Fill in the left column with learner responses. Then: 'Now — which piece of today's evidence connects to that observation? Look at your handouts. You have 2 minutes to find one connection and write it in your journal.' [Allow 2 minutes.] Cold-call 3 learners (aim for gender balance — use name sticks). After each, say: 'Does anyone want to add to or challenge that connection?' [WAIT TIME: 12 seconds.] Conclude by asking: 'So — the narrow capillary tube and the narrow xylem vessel — what do they have in common?' Cold-call 1 learner. Then say: 'We have a name for the forces that make water climb: adhesion — water sticking to the wall — and cohesion — water molecules sticking to each other. Write those two words and their definitions in your journal now.' [Allow 90 seconds.]
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Evidence-to-Phenomenon Mapping (T-Chart) — by explicitly mapping each piece of new evidence onto the anchoring phenomenon, learners construct explanatory links rather than memorising isolated facts. The 3-sentence journal entry ('I observed… This suggests… I am still unsure about…') is a metacognitive writing-to-learn strategy that consolidates understanding and surfaces remaining gaps — feeding directly into the Driving Question Board.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher reads 5–6 journal entries during the DQB phase (below) while learners are writing on the board. Specific indicator: the evidence statement should name at least one structure (xylem or root hair cell) AND at least one force (adhesion or cohesion) AND connect both to the phenomenon. If fewer than half the class achieves this, teacher opens Lesson 3 with a targeted re-teach of the structural–mechanical link.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner receives two sticky notes. On the green note, they write one thing today's evidence has helped them understand about the driving question: 'How does a maize plant move water from soil to its topmost leaves?' On the orange note, they write one new question today's evidence has raised. Learners post both notes on the class DQB (a large sheet of paper divided into: 'What we now have evidence for' / 'Questions we still need to answer'). The teacher reads 5–6 notes aloud, groups similar questions, and explicitly connects them to the upcoming lessons in the sequence (e.g., 'Three of you asked about what drives water ALL the way up — that is exactly what Lesson 3 is about').
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute sticky notes. Say: 'Green note — one thing today's evidence helped you understand. Orange note — one new question it raised. You have 3 minutes. Write in full sentences.' [Allow 3 minutes.] Invite learners to post notes on the DQB. Read 5–6 aloud (read the question, do NOT answer it yet). Group similar questions with a bracket. Say: 'Look at these orange questions — many of you are asking HOW exactly water gets pulled all the way to the top of a tall maize stalk. That is the cohesion-tension theory, and it is the focus of Lesson 3. Hold those questions — they are exactly the right ones.' Point to the driving question posted at the top of the DQB and say: 'We have not fully answered this yet — but today's evidence has moved us forward. What part can we now answer with confidence?' Cold-call 2 learners. [WAIT TIME: 15 seconds each.]
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Two-Colour Sticky-Note DQB — separating 'evidence-based understanding' (green) from 'new questions' (orange) makes the distinction between claims and evidence explicit, and models scientific practice. Reading questions aloud without answering them signals that questions are intellectually valued, motivating continued inquiry. Grouping similar questions demonstrates the power of collective sensemaking and previews the lesson sequence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher reads all posted sticky notes after class. Specific indicators: green notes should reference at least one observable structure or demonstrated force; orange notes should be genuine mechanistic questions (e.g., 'What pulls the water upward?') rather than factual recall questions (e.g., 'What is xylem?'). A prevalence of factual questions signals that learners have not yet moved from description to causal reasoning — teacher adjusts Lesson 3 opening accordingly.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners retrieve their Lesson 1 initial model (a sketch showing how they thought water moved from soil to leaf). Using a different colour pen, they annotate or redraw their model to incorporate today's evidence, adding: (a) root hair cells at the soil-root interface; (b) xylem vessels in the stem (narrow tubes in the correct position relative to phloem); (c) an arrow labelled 'adhesion' (water-to-wall) and 'cohesion' (water-to-water) inside the xylem. Learners do NOT need to be correct about the mechanism yet — the goal is to update the model with structural evidence. They write one sentence below the model: 'My model changed because today I saw evidence that…'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Get out your Lesson 1 model. Pick up a different colour pen — any colour that is NOT the one you used in Lesson 1. You are going to update your model with today's evidence. You have 7 minutes. Add at least three new things: root hair cells, xylem vessels, and the labels adhesion and cohesion. You do not need to know exactly how it works yet — just add what you have observed.' [Set timer for 7 minutes. Circulate. Coach 3–4 learners individually: 'Where in your model would you place the xylem? Think back to the cross-section diagram.' At 5 minutes, say: 'One minute left — write your sentence at the bottom: My model changed because today I saw evidence that…'] At the close, ask 2 learners to hold up their revised model and describe one change to the class. Affirm: 'Notice how Wanjiru has drawn the xylem as a narrow tube — that connects directly to what we saw in the capillary demonstration.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision with Colour-Coded Layering — using a different colour pen creates a visible record of how understanding evolves across lessons, making the learning progression tangible for both learner and teacher. The sentence stem 'My model changed because today I saw evidence that…' enforces evidence-based reasoning rather than copying from a textbook. Models will be revisited and further annotated in Lessons 3–8, ultimately becoming a complete mechanistic model of water and nutrient transport in a maize plant.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher collects or photographs 6–8 models. Specific indicators: (1) Root hair cells drawn at root surface — not inside root; (2) Xylem drawn as hollow/tube-like structures in the stem; (3) At least one force label (adhesion or cohesion) present. These models serve as a pre-assessment baseline for Lesson 3's mechanistic content. Models with xylem absent or phloem/xylem confused will receive targeted feedback at the start of Lesson 3.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: (1) Did learners correctly identify xylem (not phloem) as the tissue stained red in the phenomenon? If many confused the two, prepare a 5-minute side-by-side comparison at the start of Lesson 3. (2) Did the capillary demonstration generate genuine 'aha' moments, or did learners watch it passively? If passive, in future lessons add a prediction step with individual mini-whiteboards before the demo begins. (3) Were the orange DQB questions mechanistic (asking 'how' or 'why') or merely factual ('what is…')? If mainly factual, Lesson 3 should begin with a structured 'Notice and Wonder' routine rather than jumping directly to the cohesion-tension theory. (4) Were learners from all groups (including those who struggle with English scientific vocabulary) able to access the photomicrographs? If not, consider pairing Swahili-language captions with the diagrams in the handout for the next lesson. (5) Did you manage time effectively across the three activities in Phase 2? The capillary demonstration is the most time-sensitive — if it ran short, prioritise it first in a future iteration.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Photomicrographs of root hair cells and transverse sections of root and stem showing xylem and phloem; a live capillary-tube demonstration using red food dye showing water rising higher in narrower tubes; six gallery-walk diagrams showing cell structures and molecular forces.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Root hair cells have a large surface area that maximises water absorption from the soil. Xylem vessels are narrow, hollow, dead cells arranged in rings or bundles in the stem — these are the channels the red dye travels through in the phenomenon. Phloem is distinct from xylem and carries dissolved sugars. Adhesion (water sticking to xylem walls) and cohesion (water molecules sticking to each other) are the physical forces that help water rise in narrow tubes — just as water rises higher in a narrower capillary tube.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The red-stained rings in the cross-sectionally cut maize stem from Kisumu are xylem vessels — not phloem or any other tissue. Water is able to enter these narrow vessels partly because of adhesive and cohesive forces, analogous to the capillary rise seen in the demonstration. Root hair cells increase the surface area available for water absorption from the soil. These structural observations begin to explain how water moves upward against gravity, though the full mechanism (cohesion-tension theory, transpiration pull) will be established in Lesson 3.
