LESSONS.title: Absorption of Water and Mineral Salts: Osmosis, Active Transport, and Root Pressure

slo.purpose: To explain how water and mineral salts are absorbed by root hair cells and transported upward through the plant using osmosis, active transport, and root pressure mechanisms.
slo.knowledge: Learners describe absorption of water and mineral salts in plants (KICD SLO a), explaining the roles of osmosis, active transport, and root pressure in moving substances from the soil into and up the root.
slo.skills: Learners use print and/or digital media to research how mineral salts such as DAP (Di-ammonium Phosphate) enter root hair cells; they construct written explanations linking evidence from the red-dye phenomenon to the mechanisms discovered [SEP: Constructing Explanations].
slo.attitudes: Learners appreciate the role of transport in plants (KICD SLO e) and the importance of responsible fertiliser use — including DAP, CAN, and Urea — in sustaining maize and sukuma wiki production on Kenyan farms.
slo.keyInquiry: Why is transport in plants important?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lesson 1 learners observed that red dye travels upward through specific woody channels in the maize stem, and in Lesson 2 they gathered evidence on xylem and phloem structure. Lesson 3 now asks: HOW does water first get INTO the root and then get PUSHED up into those channels? Learners construct explanations for the entry of water (osmosis), the entry of mineral salts (active transport), and the initial upward push (root pressure) — directly answering why the dye moved up rather than staying at the bottom of the beaker.
slo.safetyNotes: No hazardous chemicals are used in this lesson. If printed diagrams are laminated, handle laminator with care. Remind learners not to ingest any food dye or salt solutions used for demonstration purposes. Wash hands after handling soil or plant specimens brought in from the school garden.

LESSONS.overview: Lesson 3 is the EXPLAIN phase of the evidence-gathering sequence. Building on the red-dye and polythene-bag phenomena from Lessons 1 and 2, learners now construct scientific explanations for HOW water and mineral salts enter a maize root and begin their upward journey. Through a structured Predict-first discussion, a guided jigsaw research task using print/digital media, and a whole-class sensemaking discussion, learners distinguish between osmosis (water entry via a concentration gradient across the semi-permeable root hair cell membrane), active transport (energy-requiring uptake of mineral ions such as phosphate from DAP fertiliser), and root pressure (the resulting hydrostatic push that drives water up into the xylem). Kenyan agricultural context — fertiliser use on maize and sukuma wiki farms in Rift Valley, Kisumu, and Central Kenya — is woven throughout. Learners close by updating the Driving Question Board and revising their cumulative transport model.
LESSONS.aresKeywords: osmosis, active transport, root pressure, root hair cells, semi-permeable membrane, concentration gradient, mineral salts, DAP fertiliser, xylem, phloem, translocation, maize, sukuma wiki, Kenya, water potential, solute potential, turgor, plasmolysis, diffusion, ATP, mineral uptake

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the red-dye observation from Lesson 1: the dye moved upward through the maize stem against gravity. The teacher displays a large printed photograph of a maize root hair cell diagram alongside a jar of soil-water (murky water with dissolved salts) and a jar of plain water. Learners individually write a 2-sentence prediction in their science notebooks answering: 'The water inside a root hair cell is less/more concentrated than the water in the soil — therefore water will move IN/OUT of the cell.' They then share predictions with a shoulder partner (Think-Pair) before three cold-calls to the class. Learners also predict whether a maize plant fertilised with DAP near Kericho would absorb more or fewer mineral ions than an unfertilised plant, and why.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the two jars and the root hair cell diagram on the board or projector. Say: 'Look carefully at these two solutions. Before I tell you anything new today, I want you to think about what you already believe.' Pause for 30 seconds of silent thinking. Then instruct: 'Write your prediction — two sentences — NOW. You have 90 seconds.' After writing, say: 'Turn to your partner. You have 60 seconds each.' After pair-share, cold-call exactly THREE learners using name cards or a random selector. For each response, ask one follow-up probe: 'What evidence from our Lesson 1 observation makes you say that?' Allow 10–12 seconds WAIT TIME after each cold-call before accepting an answer. Record contrasting predictions (water moves IN vs. water moves OUT) in two columns on the board labelled PREDICT — leave these visible throughout the lesson for revisiting. Do NOT correct predictions at this stage.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think-Pair-Share Prediction Wall. By externalising individual predictions before instruction, learners activate prior knowledge of concentration and diffusion from Junior School Integrated Science. The visible two-column Prediction Wall creates cognitive dissonance that motivates the research task and gives the teacher real-time diagnostic data on misconceptions (e.g., learners who predict water moves OUT of the root).
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Every learner has produced a written 2-sentence prediction in their notebook within the 90-second window. The teacher scans notebooks during the pair-share, noting (a) learners who correctly predict inward osmosis, (b) learners who confuse direction, and (c) learners who cannot explain using concentration. These three groups inform targeted questioning during the Explain phase. Target: ≥80% of learners produce a written prediction that uses the word 'concentrated' or 'concentration' even if the direction is wrong.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in groups of four. Each group receives one laminated ARES resource card (or accesses the ARES offline digital module) covering one of four topics: (A) Osmosis and Water Potential in Root Hair Cells, (B) Active Transport of Mineral Ions — Focus on Phosphate from DAP, (C) Root Pressure and the Hydrostatic Push into Xylem, (D) Consequences of Fertiliser Overuse — Plasmolysis and Wilting in Sukuma Wiki. Groups read/view their resource for 8 minutes, then each group member becomes an 'expert' who will teach the other three. After 3 minutes of individual note-taking on a structured Evidence Record sheet (three columns: What I observed/read | What it means | Connection to our maize phenomenon), jigsaw groups of four (one expert per topic) form and each expert teaches their topic in 2 minutes. All learners complete their Evidence Record sheet across all four topics. The teacher circulates and listens to jigsaw teaching for accuracy.
framework.teacherMoves: Before releasing groups, say: 'Your job is not just to read — your job is to gather EVIDENCE that will help you explain why the red dye moved up through those wooden rings in our maize stem. Every fact you find must connect back to that stem.' Distribute or open resource cards. Set a visible countdown timer for 8 minutes (reading) + 3 minutes (individual notes) + 8 minutes (jigsaw teaching). Circulate during jigsaw teaching. Stop at Group B discussions and ask: 'When a Rift Valley farmer adds DAP fertiliser to the soil, what happens to the concentration of phosphate ions around the root — does it go UP or DOWN?' Wait 10 seconds. Cold-call one learner from the group. Stop at Group D discussions and ask: 'A sukuma wiki farmer in Kiambu over-applies CAN fertiliser. She notices the leaves wilting the next morning even though she watered the night before. What does your evidence card say about why this might happen?' Wait 12 seconds before accepting an answer. After jigsaw teaching, bring the class back together. Write the three key terms on the board: OSMOSIS | ACTIVE TRANSPORT | ROOT PRESSURE. Say: 'In the next phase, you are going to use these three ideas to explain our phenomenon — so hold onto your Evidence Record sheets.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Expert Jigsaw with Anchored Evidence Records. The jigsaw structure ensures every learner encounters all four topics while developing accountability as a peer teacher. The Evidence Record sheet's third column ('Connection to our maize phenomenon') forces learners to continuously tether new information to the anchoring phenomenon rather than treating it as disconnected facts. This is a core NGSS SEP: Obtaining, Evaluating, and Communicating Information scaffold.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Each learner's Evidence Record sheet has at least one entry in all three columns for each of the four topics by the end of the jigsaw. The teacher spot-checks five to six sheets during circulation, specifically checking Column 3 (connection to phenomenon). Learners who leave Column 3 blank are prompted: 'How does this help you explain what happened in our maize stem on Day 1?' Additionally, the teacher listens for accuracy during jigsaw teaching — if a Group B expert incorrectly describes active transport as passive, the teacher intervenes with a Socratic prompt: 'Does this process require the plant to spend energy — yes or no? Where does that energy come from?'

framework.learnerExperience: Whole class reconvenes. The teacher uses a large annotated diagram of a maize root cross-section (projected or drawn on the board) showing: soil water, root hair cell with vacuole, cell membrane, cortex cells, endodermis (Casparian strip), and xylem vessel. Working in their original groups, learners construct a written Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) explanation answering: 'How does water from the soil in our Kisumu school garden reach the xylem vessel of a maize plant — and how does it then get pushed upward?' Each group writes on a shared A3 sheet. Groups then share key sentences with the class in a gallery-walk format (sheets posted on wall, learners rotate for 3 minutes, adding sticky-note agreements or challenges). The teacher leads a 10-minute whole-class discussion synthesising the three mechanisms, correcting misconceptions, and explicitly connecting each mechanism back to the red-dye observation. Specific connection: 'Root pressure is the pump — it is why the red dye we saw moved UP into the stem, not just sideways.' Learners also discuss why DAP (Di-ammonium Phosphate) fertiliser, widely used on maize farms in Uasin Gishu and Trans-Nzoia, improves absorption — because active transport carriers in root hair cells take up phosphate and ammonium ions, improving overall water potential gradients.
framework.teacherMoves: Introduce CER explicitly: 'A scientific explanation has three parts. Claim — your answer. Evidence — data or observations that support it. Reasoning — the science principle that links them.' Write CER on the board with a maize-farm example: 'Claim: Water enters the root hair cell from the soil. Evidence: In Lesson 1, the red dye moved upward. Reasoning: Osmosis — water moves from high water potential (soil) to low water potential (root cell vacuole) across the semi-permeable membrane.' Give groups exactly 7 minutes to write their CER on A3 paper. During gallery walk, prompt readers with: 'What is the EVIDENCE in this group's explanation? Is it from our observations or from the resource cards?' After gallery walk, lead synthesis: point to the root diagram and trace the journey — soil → root hair → cortex → xylem — narrating each mechanism aloud. At the xylem entry point, say: 'This build-up of water in the xylem creates pressure — ROOT PRESSURE. This is the first engine that pushes water up. Does this help us explain our red dye going UP against gravity?' Cold-call TWO learners. Wait 12 seconds each. Then ask: 'Why would a maize farmer in Eldoret who never adds DAP see slower water transport than one who does?' Cold-call ONE learner. Accept answers, then clarify: phosphate ions enter via active transport, increasing solute concentration in root cells, steepening the osmotic gradient and enhancing water uptake. Explicitly revisit the Prediction Wall: 'Look at our predictions from earlier. Who had the right direction for osmosis — and who needs to revise?' Ask learners to place a self-stick dot on the correct prediction column.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) Framework + Gallery Walk. CER structures scientific writing so learners do not simply restate facts but explicitly justify them using evidence. The gallery walk introduces peer critique as a sensemaking tool — learners must evaluate whether another group's evidence is valid (from observations) or merely asserted. The public revisit of the Prediction Wall closes the predict-observe-explain loop, making conceptual change visible to learners themselves.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Each group's CER sheet contains (a) an explicit claim naming at least two of the three mechanisms (osmosis, active transport, root pressure), (b) at least one piece of evidence traceable to either the Lesson 1 phenomenon or the Lesson 2/3 research, and (c) a reasoning statement that uses a scientific principle (e.g., concentration gradient, semi-permeable membrane, ATP). The teacher collects all A3 sheets. Any CER that lacks a reasoning statement is flagged for targeted feedback before Lesson 4. Additionally, the self-stick dot activity gives the teacher a rapid visual of how many learners (target: ≥75%) correctly self-identify the inward direction of osmosis after instruction.

framework.learnerExperience: The teacher displays the class Driving Question Board, which carries the anchoring question and sticky notes from Lessons 1 and 2. Learners individually write NEW sticky notes (green = new explanations, orange = new questions that arose today). Each learner posts at least one green note and one orange note. Sample green notes expected: 'Water enters root hair cells by osmosis because the cell sap is more concentrated than soil water'; 'DAP fertiliser adds phosphate ions that are pulled in by active transport using ATP'; 'Root pressure pushes water up into the xylem — that is why the dye rose.' Sample orange notes expected: 'If root pressure starts the push, what keeps the water going up to the topmost maize leaf — is root pressure enough?'; 'Why does the dye only go into the xylem rings and not the phloem?'; 'What happens if the soil becomes too salty from too much fertiliser?' The class briefly reviews the board together: the teacher groups related notes and identifies the most important unresolved question, which becomes the bridge to Lesson 4 (translocation and the cohesion-tension mechanism).
framework.teacherMoves: Hand each learner two sticky notes (one green, one orange — or use different coloured pens on the same colour note). Say: 'Green notes are for things we can NOW explain. Orange notes are for new questions your brain is asking — things today's lesson did NOT fully answer.' Allow 3 minutes of silent individual writing. Then say: 'Walk up, post your notes, and read two others before you sit down.' After posting, stand at the DQB and narrate aloud: 'Look — many of us are now asking: root pressure explains the START of the journey, but a maize plant in Kisumu grows two metres tall. Is root pressure strong enough to push water all the way to the top leaf? That is exactly where Lesson 4 takes us.' Point to any orange notes about 'too much fertiliser' and say: 'This connects to what we said about CAN and DAP — over-applying fertiliser reverses the osmotic gradient. We called that PLASMOLYSIS. Remember that word — it will appear again in Plant Growth.' Do NOT answer the Lesson 4 questions now — preserve genuine inquiry tension.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Two-Colour DQB Protocol (Explain vs. Question). Separating new explanations (green) from new questions (orange) makes the asymmetry between current understanding and remaining unknowns visible on a single board. This metacognitive tool helps learners see that science is cumulative — each lesson resolves some questions and opens new ones — and it creates authentic motivation for the next lesson in the sequence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Every learner posts at least one green note containing a mechanistic explanation (not merely a label). The teacher scans green notes for naïve explanations such as 'water goes in because plants need water' — these lack mechanism and are earmarked for follow-up. Orange notes that identify the cohesion-tension gap ('root pressure is not enough for tall plants') indicate higher-order thinking and can be used to accelerate instruction in Lesson 4. Collect a photo of the DQB for the ARES platform record.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners retrieve their transport model diagram from Lesson 2 (a sketch of the maize plant showing the xylem pathway). They now REVISE and ANNOTATE it to add the root-level mechanisms explained today. Required additions: (1) Root hair cell with arrows showing water entering by osmosis (labelled with 'high water potential → low water potential'); (2) Active transport carriers on the root hair cell membrane with ATP lightning bolt symbols, showing mineral ion (phosphate/NH₄⁺) entry; (3) A ROOT PRESSURE arrow inside the xylem pointing upward; (4) A soil annotation noting 'DAP fertiliser increases phosphate concentration in soil — active transport required.' Learners also write a one-sentence MODEL LIMITATION note at the bottom: 'This model does not yet explain how water continues rising above the root — that is the next question.' Revised models are initialled by a peer before being stored in the ARES portfolio.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute or ask learners to open their Lesson 2 model sketches. Say: 'Your model from Lesson 2 showed WHERE water travels in the plant. Today you are adding HOW it gets in at the root level. A better model explains mechanism, not just structure.' Project a sample annotated root hair cell on the board (without the labels filled in) as a scaffold. Say: 'You have 8 minutes. Add at least FOUR new annotations to your model — I will come around and check.' Circulate and prompt: 'Show me where osmosis is happening on your diagram.' 'Where is energy being used? Mark it.' 'If a farmer adds too much urea near these roots, what would happen to your water potential arrows — would they reverse?' Allow a 2-minute peer-initialling swap at the end. Collect five to six models for formative review before Lesson 4. Close the lesson by asking the class: 'Our model now explains the root. But look at this maize plant photo — the water still has to climb two metres. What is pulling it up? That is our next investigation.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Iterative Model Annotation (Progressive Model Building). Requiring learners to annotate rather than redraw forces them to reconcile new mechanistic knowledge with their existing structural model, promoting conceptual integration. The 'Model Limitation' sentence is a deliberate metacognitive move — it teaches learners that a good scientific model explicitly acknowledges what it cannot yet explain, mirroring authentic scientific practice (NGSS SEP: Developing and Using Models). The peer initialling introduces low-stakes peer assessment.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Revised models contain all four required additions. The teacher specifically checks that osmosis arrows are drawn in the correct direction (soil → root hair cell) and that active transport is distinguished from osmosis by the presence of an energy marker (ATP symbol or the word 'energy required'). Models where osmosis arrows are reversed or where active transport is labelled as diffusion are flagged. During Lesson 4 warm-up, the teacher returns two or three anonymised flagged models to the class for whole-group revision as a re-teaching moment.

LESSONS.teacherReflection:
After the lesson, reflect on the following questions in your ARES teacher journal:
1. PREDICTION WALL — How many learners initially predicted the wrong direction for osmosis (water OUT of the root)? Did the lesson successfully shift this misconception? What evidence (sticky dots, CER sheets, model arrows) confirms the shift?
2. JIGSAW QUALITY — Were learners able to accurately teach their assigned topic to peers, or did certain topics (e.g., active transport and ATP; root pressure mechanism) produce inaccurate peer-teaching? Which resource cards may need to be simplified or supplemented with a short teacher-led mini-explanation before Lesson 4?
3. KENYA CONTEXT INTEGRATION — Did learners make genuine connections between DAP/CAN fertiliser use and the mechanisms of mineral salt absorption, or did the agricultural context feel grafted on? Consider whether a brief visit to the school's own kitchen garden (if applicable) or a photo gallery of Trans-Nzoia maize farms would deepen engagement in Lesson 4.
4. CER DEPTH — Scan the A3 CER sheets collected. Were reasoning statements mechanistic (referencing concentration gradients, semi-permeable membranes, ATP) or surface-level ('because plants need water')? Plan a 5-minute CER quality warm-up at the start of Lesson 4 using an anonymised strong example and an anonymised weak example.
5. DQB ORANGE NOTES — Count how many orange notes correctly identify the cohesion-tension gap (root pressure alone insufficient for a 2-metre maize plant). This is the conceptual readiness indicator for Lesson 4. If fewer than half the class produced this question organically, plan an explicit hook at the start of Lesson 4 — e.g., 'Root pressure generates about 0.1–0.2 MPa. A 2-metre maize plant needs approximately 0.2 MPa just to overcome gravity. So we are right at the limit — what else must be happening?'

summaryTablePrompt.observed: In Lesson 1 we observed that red food dye placed in a beaker of water entered the roots of a freshly uprooted maize seedling from our Kisumu school garden and moved upward, appearing as vivid red rings only inside the xylem tissue when the stem was cut cross-sectionally. In Lesson 2 we identified the xylem and phloem as the transport channels. In today's lesson we examined diagrams and research resources showing root hair cells in contact with soil water, and we observed that the cell sap inside the root hair cell vacuole is more concentrated (lower water potential) than the water in the surrounding soil.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Water enters root hair cells by OSMOSIS — it moves from a region of higher water potential (dilute soil water) to a region of lower water potential (concentrated cell sap) across the semi-permeable cell membrane. Mineral salts such as phosphate ions from DAP fertiliser and ammonium ions from CAN or Urea cannot enter by osmosis; they are absorbed by ACTIVE TRANSPORT — protein carrier molecules in the cell membrane use ATP energy to pump ions against their concentration gradient into the root hair cell. As water and mineral ions accumulate in the root cells and pass inward through the cortex to the xylem, they create a hydrostatic pressure called ROOT PRESSURE, which pushes water upward into and through the xylem vessels. This is why the red dye in our phenomenon moved upward against gravity. Over-application of fertiliser increases solute concentration in the soil, reversing the water potential gradient and causing water to leave the root cells (plasmolysis), which is why sukuma wiki or maize can wilt after excess fertiliser is applied.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The red dye entered the maize root and rose through the xylem because: (1) osmosis drove water molecules from the relatively dilute soil water into the more concentrated root hair cell vacuole across the semi-permeable membrane; (2) active transport used ATP to pump mineral ions such as phosphate (from DAP) into the root cells against their concentration gradient, further lowering water potential and sustaining the osmotic gradient; and (3) the accumulation of water in the xylem generated root pressure — a hydrostatic push that propelled the dye-coloured water upward through the xylem channels, which is why only the xylem rings (not the phloem or pith) turned red. Our model now explains the ROOT END of the journey. However, root pressure alone may not be sufficient to lift water to the topmost leaves of a two-metre maize plant — this is the unresolved question we carry into Lesson 4.

LESSONS.title: Translocation: How Does the Maize Plant Move Sugar from Leaf to Root?

slo.purpose: Learners will explain the process of translocation in plants by analysing evidence from a ring-barking (girdling) demonstration and comparing xylem and phloem function, connecting their findings to the anchoring phenomenon of how the Kisumu maize plant moves substances from source to sink.
slo.knowledge: Learners explain translocation in plants, describing the source-to-sink model of phloem transport and distinguishing between the roles of xylem (water and mineral salts, upward) and phloem (sugars and assimilates, bidirectional, source to sink).
slo.skills: Learners analyse and interpret data from a ring-barking/girdling demonstration; construct explanations for why the coloured-water dye in the anchoring phenomenon moves only through xylem tissue; complete a two-column xylem-vs-phloem comparison chart; and update the Driving Question Board with translocation evidence. [SEP: Analysing and Interpreting Data; Constructing Explanations]
slo.attitudes: Learners appreciate the role of transport in plants — including translocation — in sustaining plant life, crop productivity, and food security for Kenyan farmers in regions such as Kisumu, Kericho, and the Rift Valley.
slo.keyInquiry: Why is transport in plants important?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lessons 1–3 learners established that water and mineral salts move upward through xylem vessels (demonstrated by the red-dye maize experiment). Lesson 4 now asks: what about the sugars made by photosynthesis in the leaves — how do they reach the roots, the developing maize cob, or the growing tip? By observing the girdling demonstration and analysing phloem exudate evidence, learners discover the second transport tissue — phloem — and the source-to-sink model. This advances the driving question by explaining not only HOW water moves up, but HOW manufactured food moves to where it is needed throughout the plant.
slo.safetyNotes: Razor blades or scalpels used in the ring-barking demonstration must be handled only by the teacher or a designated learner under direct supervision. Freshly cut stem surfaces may be slippery — place specimens in a tray. Learners must wash hands after handling plant material. No open wounds near cut plant surfaces. If using a bean or sweet-potato stem, avoid touching eyes after handling. All sharp instruments to be collected and counted at the end of the lesson.

LESSONS.overview: Learners begin by revisiting their Driving Question Board and predicting what tissue carries sugar from a maize leaf down to the roots and developing cob. The teacher then leads a ring-barking (girdling) demonstration on a soft-stemmed plant (e.g., a bean or sweet-potato cutting from the school garden), directing learners to observe the swelling of tissue just above the ring cut over time (or via pre-prepared specimens showing the swelling). Learners also examine photographic/diagrammatic evidence of phloem exudate from aphid stylet experiments and sieve-tube diagrams. Using an Analysing-and-Interpreting-Data routine, pairs record observations in a structured data table, then use a two-column Xylem-vs-Phloem chart to construct an explanation. A source-to-sink model is introduced through a worked example using a maize plant (leaves as source, roots and cob as sinks). Learners then construct written explanations linking both the red-dye xylem evidence (Lessons 1–3) and the new phloem/girdling evidence to the driving question. The DQB is updated collectively. The lesson closes with a teacher-facilitated sensemaking discussion tying translocation to the real-world importance of watering, manuring, and fertilising crops on Kenyan farms.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners individually write a prediction (2–3 sentences) in their science journals answering: 'In a maize plant growing on a farm near Kisumu, the leaves make sugar by photosynthesis. Predict: how does that sugar reach the roots and the developing maize cob? Does it travel through the same red-stained channels we saw in Lesson 2, or through different channels — and why do you think so?' Learners share predictions with a shoulder partner (Think-Pair) for 2 minutes, then three learners are cold-called to share aloud.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the anchoring phenomenon image (cross-section of maize stem showing red-stained xylem rings) on the board alongside a diagram of a maize plant with arrows labelled 'sugar made here' at the leaves and question marks at the roots and cob. Say: 'In our last lessons we tracked water moving UP through those red rings. Today we ask a different question — what about the food the plant makes? Where does it go, and how?' Distribute science journals. Give learners 3 minutes of individual silent writing time. After Think-Pair, cold-call exactly 3 learners using name sticks: ask each 'What evidence from our previous lessons supports your prediction?' WAIT 12 seconds after each prompt before accepting an answer. Record key prediction terms (e.g., 'same tubes,' 'different tubes,' 'phloem,' 'flows down') on the board without evaluating correctness — label the board column 'Our Predictions (Lesson 4).'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think-Pair-Predict: activates prior knowledge of xylem from Lessons 1–3 and creates cognitive dissonance — learners who predicted 'same tubes' will be productively challenged by the girdling evidence in the Observe phase. Recording predictions publicly ensures accountability and revisiting.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher circulates during individual writing and notes (on a clipboard checklist) whether learners: (a) reference xylem by name, (b) propose a different tissue for sugar, or (c) give no tissue-specific answer. This identifies who needs targeted questioning during the Observe phase. Observable indicator: at least 70% of learners write a prediction that references a specific plant tissue.

framework.learnerExperience: PART A — Ring-Barking Demonstration (15 min): The teacher (or designated learner under supervision) shows two pre-prepared bean or sweet-potato stem specimens: Specimen A — intact stem; Specimen B — a stem that was ring-barked (a 1–2 cm band of bark/phloem removed) 48 hours earlier, showing visible swelling/bulging of tissue just above the cut. Learners sketch both specimens in their journals, labelling the cut zone, the swelling above, and the region below. They record: 'What is different between specimen A and specimen B? Where is the swelling, and what might have accumulated there?' PART B — Phloem Evidence Cards (10 min): Learners work in pairs to analyse two Evidence Cards (printed A5 sheets prepared by the teacher): Card 1 shows a labelled diagram of a sieve tube and companion cell with arrows indicating direction of flow; Card 2 shows a photograph and description of aphid stylet experiments (aphid inserts stylet into phloem, sugary sap flows out — used as evidence that phloem carries sugars under pressure). Pairs complete a structured Observation Data Table: Column 1 — Observation (what I see/read); Column 2 — What this tells me about phloem. PART C — Xylem-vs-Phloem Two-Column Chart (5 min): Each learner independently fills in a partially completed two-column chart comparing xylem and phloem across five attributes: tissue type, contents transported, direction of movement, cell structure (living/dead), and driving force.
framework.teacherMoves: Before showing Specimen B, ask: 'Look carefully at the area just above the ring cut. What do you notice?' WAIT 12 seconds. Cold-call 2 learners. Then ask: 'If water was accumulating here, where would it have come from? But wait — water moves UP through xylem. So what else might be accumulating ABOVE the cut?' WAIT 15 seconds — this is the key productive-struggle moment; do not answer immediately. After learners propose ideas, say: 'You are thinking like scientists. Let us look at our Evidence Cards to test your ideas.' During pair work on Evidence Cards, circulate and ask probing questions: 'On Card 2, the aphid stylet goes INTO the stem — which layer does it reach? What does the sugary sap tell us about what phloem carries?' After pairs complete their data tables, project a blank two-column chart on the board and ask pairs to contribute one row each using a round-robin format. Validate each row with: 'Does everyone agree? Give me a thumbs up if your chart matches.' Correct any misconceptions about directionality — emphasise: 'Xylem is one-way — soil to leaf. Phloem is source-to-sink — wherever sugar is made TO wherever sugar is needed.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Analysing and Interpreting Data (NGSS SEP 4): Learners move from raw observation (swelling above ring cut) to inference (phloem must carry something that cannot pass the cut) to pattern recognition (phloem moves substances from source to sink). The structured data table scaffolds this progression explicitly, preventing learners from jumping to conclusions without evidence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher checks completed Observation Data Tables during circulation — look for: (a) correct identification of swelling above (not below) the cut, (b) inference that phloem carries sugars/assimilates downward, (c) at least 3 of 5 rows correctly completed in the two-column chart. Cold-call one pair per Evidence Card to share their 'What this tells me' column. Observable indicator: pairs correctly identify the direction of phloem transport (source → sink) and name sugars/assimilates as phloem contents.

framework.learnerExperience: PART A — Source-to-Sink Mapping (10 min): Learners receive a printed outline diagram of a maize plant (roots, stem, leaves, developing cob). Working individually, they label: (i) two SOURCES of sugar (mature leaves), (ii) three SINKS (roots, developing cob, young growing leaves at the apex), and (iii) draw arrows showing the direction of phloem transport from each source to each sink. They also draw a separate set of arrows showing xylem transport direction, using a different colour. PART B — Written Explanation (10 min): Learners write a 4–6 sentence explanation in their journals connecting BOTH the red-dye xylem evidence (from Lessons 1–3) AND the girdling evidence (today) to the driving question: 'How does a maize plant move water and nutrients from the soil all the way to its topmost leaves — and what does it do with the food it makes?' They must use the terms: xylem, phloem, translocation, source, sink, sieve tube, companion cell, and cohesion-tension (revision from Lesson 3). PART C — Peer Plenary Share (5 min): Three learners (cold-called) read their explanations aloud. Class listens and gives one 'star' (something strong) and one 'step' (something to improve) using a structured peer-feedback protocol.
framework.teacherMoves: Introduce the source-to-sink model with a Kenyan farming analogy: 'Think of a maize farm in Kisumu. The leaves are like the posho mill — they produce the food (ugali flour = sugar). The roots and the cob are like the market stalls — they receive and use the food. The phloem is like the matatu route connecting the mill to the market.' Write the analogy on the board. Then say: 'Use this model to label your maize diagram. Remember: a SOURCE is wherever sugar is MADE or STORED and then released; a SINK is wherever sugar is USED or STORED.' During individual writing, circulate and prompt struggling learners: 'You described xylem in Lesson 2 — can you now write one sentence that CONTRASTS phloem with xylem?' For the plenary, after each cold-called learner reads, ask the class: 'Did they include the word TRANSLOCATION? Did they explain the direction clearly?' WAIT 10 seconds. Correct any conflation of transpiration and translocation — say: 'Transpiration is water LEAVING the plant through stomata. Translocation is food MOVING inside the plant through phloem. Different process, different tissue, different purpose.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Constructing Explanations (NGSS SEP 6): Learners synthesise two independent lines of evidence (red-dye xylem experiment + girdling demonstration) into a single coherent explanation that advances the driving question. The Kenyan matatu/posho mill analogy provides a culturally grounded conceptual anchor that makes the abstract source-to-sink model concrete and memorable.
framework.formativeAssessment: Collect written explanations (or photograph journal pages) as an exit artefact. Assess against three criteria: (1) correct use of 'translocation' to describe phloem transport, (2) correct directionality (source → sink), (3) explicit contrast with xylem transport. Observable indicator: at least 65% of learners produce written explanations meeting all three criteria. Peer feedback round gives teacher real-time data on class-wide understanding.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class Driving Question Board (a large poster or section of the board maintained across all 8 lessons). In pairs, they write one new sticky note each: a GREEN note stating one new thing they can NOW explain about the maize plant's transport system (using evidence from today's lesson), and an ORANGE note stating one question that TODAY's lesson raised but has not yet answered (e.g., 'What powers phloem transport — is it pressure or something else?' or 'Does the maize plant always move sugar downward, or can it go upward too?'). Pairs post their notes and one representative per pair reads their green note aloud to the class.
framework.teacherMoves: Point to the driving question displayed prominently: 'How does a maize plant move water and nutrients from the soil all the way to its topmost leaves — and what happens to that water in the end?' Say: 'After four lessons, let us audit what we can now explain — and what remains mysterious.' Give pairs 4 minutes to write their sticky notes. As pairs post notes, group the green notes into two clusters on the board: 'XYLEM evidence' and 'PHLOEM evidence.' Say: 'Look — we now have TWO transport systems mapped. Our first three lessons gave us the xylem half of the story. Today gave us the phloem half.' Read two or three orange notes aloud and say: 'These are excellent scientific questions. We will return to some of them in Lessons 5 and 6 when we investigate transpiration.' Link explicitly to the second part of the anchoring phenomenon: 'Remember the polythene bag with water droplets? The water vapour came from XYLEM water leaving through stomata — transpiration. Our next lesson will investigate that. But today's lesson explained what happens to the SUGAR — it travels through PHLOEM by translocation.' WAIT 10 seconds after posing: 'Can anyone now explain why ring-barking a tree in Kericho eventually kills it, even though its xylem is undamaged?' Cold-call 2 learners.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board Curation: making thinking visible across the 8-lesson sequence. Green/orange sticky-note protocol separates 'evidence we have' from 'questions still open,' mirroring how scientists distinguish established findings from ongoing inquiry. Clustering notes by tissue type makes the two-transport-system architecture of the plant visually explicit.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher scans all posted sticky notes during the plenary. Observable indicators: (a) green notes name 'phloem' or 'translocation' specifically (not vague 'tubes'), (b) orange notes reflect genuine conceptual curiosity rather than repetition of already-answered questions. Teacher flags pairs whose green notes contain misconceptions (e.g., 'phloem carries water') for targeted follow-up at lesson start of Lesson 5.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners retrieve their cumulative plant transport model diagram begun in Lesson 1 (a cross-sectional and longitudinal diagram of a maize stem and plant). Today they add the following to their model: (i) colour-in or shade the phloem tissue in a contrasting colour to xylem on the stem cross-section; (ii) draw and label sieve tubes and companion cells in the phloem region; (iii) add directional arrows for translocation (source leaves → sinks: roots, cob, apex) using a different arrow style (dashed) from xylem arrows (solid); (iv) write a model key that defines SOURCE, SINK, TRANSLOCATION, and PHLOEM. Learners then write a one-sentence 'model limitation' at the bottom: one thing their diagram does NOT yet show about phloem transport (e.g., 'My model does not show the pressure mechanism that drives phloem flow').
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute learners' model folders/booklets. Say: 'Every lesson we make our model more complete. In Lesson 1 your model showed only the outside of the maize plant. In Lesson 2 you added xylem vessels and the red-dye pathway. In Lesson 3 you added cohesion-tension forces. Today you add the SECOND transport system — phloem — and show translocation.' Project a reference diagram of a maize stem cross-section showing both xylem and phloem positions (vascular bundle). Say: 'Phloem is on the OUTER edge of the vascular bundle; xylem is on the inner edge — notice this on your cross-section.' Circulate and check: (a) arrows for phloem are going in the correct directions (not always downward — remind learners that young leaves at the apex are also sinks so phloem can move upward there too); (b) sieve tubes are labelled. After 8 minutes, cold-call one learner to hold up and describe their updated model to the class. Ask the class: 'What has this model added since Lesson 3? What is still missing?' WAIT 12 seconds. Close by saying: 'A good scientific model is honest about its limitations. Writing your model limitation is not a weakness — it is what scientists do. It tells us where our next investigation must go.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision: each lesson's model update is additive and explicitly linked to new evidence, so learners experience scientific modelling as an iterative, evidence-driven process rather than a one-off diagram. The 'model limitation' sentence develops metacognitive awareness of the difference between a model and reality — a core scientific practice.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher reviews 5–6 models during circulation (not all — use a rotating roster across lessons). Check: (a) phloem correctly positioned on vascular bundle cross-section, (b) translocation arrows correctly labelled with source/sink, (c) model limitation sentence is scientifically meaningful. Observable indicator: 70% of models reviewed show phloem arrows in at least two directions (to roots AND to apex/cob), demonstrating understanding that 'sink' is context-dependent, not always 'downward.'

LESSONS.teacherReflection:
After the lesson, reflect on the following questions in your professional journal:
1. PREDICT PHASE: Did learners' initial predictions show residual confusion between xylem and phloem from earlier lessons? If more than 40% of learners predicted 'same tubes,' consider opening Lesson 5 with a brief retrieval quiz on the two-tissue distinction before proceeding to transpiration.
2. OBSERVE PHASE: Was the swelling on the pre-prepared ring-barked specimen clearly visible? If the specimen preparation (48 hours in advance) was insufficient, consider using a photograph of ring-barking evidence from a mature tree in the school compound or a Kenyan tea bush (Camellia sinensis) from Kericho, which shows dramatic phloem girdling effects. Document any specimen preparation timeline issues for future delivery.
3. EXPLAIN PHASE: During the plenary share, did learners consistently conflate 'translocation' with 'transpiration'? If yes, create a dedicated vocabulary anchor card (posted in the classroom for the remainder of the unit) contrasting the two terms with a simple Kenyan-context mnemonic: 'TransLOcation = fLOw of food through phLoem; TransPIRation = Plant Is Releasing water vapour.'
4. DQB UPDATE: Review the orange (unanswered question) sticky notes overnight. Cluster them and use the most common themes to open Lesson 5. If many learners asked about the energy source for phloem transport, consider adding a 5-minute ATP/active-loading hook to the start of Lesson 5.
5. MODEL BUILDING: Were learners able to correctly orient phloem on the outer edge of the vascular bundle without further prompting? If not, bring in a fresh maize stem cross-section in Lesson 5 for learners to observe directly under a hand lens, reinforcing the structural claim from the model.
6. DIFFERENTIATION NOTE: Learners who completed the two-column chart quickly and accurately can be challenged with an extension question: 'A sugarcane farmer in Kisumu cuts through the stem at harvest time and notices a sweet liquid oozing from the cut. Which tissue is this liquid coming from, and how does the source-to-sink model explain why it is sweet?' This connects to real Kenyan agricultural experience and previates further organic chemistry content.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed a ring-barked (girdled) bean or sweet-potato stem where a band of outer tissue (phloem) was removed: tissue swelled and accumulated just ABOVE the cut but not below. We also analysed Evidence Cards showing sieve tubes, companion cells, and aphid stylet experiments confirming sugary sap flows under pressure through phloem.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Plants have TWO transport systems. Xylem carries water and mineral salts upward from roots to leaves (as shown by the red-dye experiment in Lessons 1–3). Phloem carries sugars and other assimilates by TRANSLOCATION from SOURCE regions (mature photosynthesising leaves) to SINK regions (roots, developing maize cob, young growing leaves) — the direction is always from where sugar is made or stored toward where it is needed. Ring-barking blocks phloem but not xylem, explaining why girdled trees eventually die even though water still reaches their leaves.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The red-stained rings in our Kisumu maize stem cross-section (the anchoring phenomenon) are XYLEM — they carry only water and mineral salts upward. The colourless outer tissue of the vascular bundle is PHLOEM — it carries sugars made by photosynthesis to the rest of the plant by translocation. Together, these two systems explain how the maize plant sustains every living cell: xylem supplies water and minerals for photosynthesis; phloem distributes the glucose produced. The polythene-bag water droplets (transpiration, second part of the phenomenon) will be fully explained in Lesson 5 — that water exits through stomata from the xylem stream.

LESSONS.title: Transpiration Experiment Setup: Designing Investigations into Factors Affecting Water Loss in Plants

slo.purpose: Learners design and set up controlled experiments to investigate how specific factors — leaf surface area (petroleum jelly), wind, humidity, and light intensity — affect the rate of transpiration in plants, thereby advancing their understanding of how water that travels upward through xylem ultimately exits the maize plant.
slo.knowledge: Learners will know that transpiration is the loss of water vapour from plant surfaces (mainly stomata); that environmental factors (wind, light, humidity) and structural factors (leaf surface area with functional stomata) influence its rate; and that a controlled investigation requires a hypothesis, identified independent/dependent/controlled variables, and an initial baseline measurement.
slo.skills: Learners will be able to: (a) state a testable hypothesis for their assigned factor; (b) correctly identify and operationalise independent, dependent, and controlled variables; (c) set up a transpiration experiment safely using locally available materials; (d) record initial measurements systematically in a results table; (e) apply SEP: Planning and Carrying Out Investigations.
slo.attitudes: Learners will appreciate the value of fair testing and collaborative roles in scientific inquiry; demonstrate unity by sharing equipment responsibly; and show responsibility by observing all safety precautions during setup.
slo.keyInquiry: Why is transport in plants important?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lessons 1–4 learners saw red dye travel upward through xylem and water droplets form inside a sealed polythene bag. They now know water moves up through xylem and exits via transpiration. But the driving question asks: what happens to that water in the end — and what controls how fast it leaves? Lesson 5 shifts from observing a teacher-led demonstration to learners themselves designing investigations. Each group manipulates one factor and sets up their experiment, making this the evidence-gathering engine that Lessons 6 and 7 will analyse and explain.
slo.safetyNotes: Petroleum jelly is non-toxic but keep away from eyes — wash hands after application. Fans (if electric) must be kept away from water sources; confirm cables are intact before use. Polythene bags must not be placed over learners' heads at any time. Scissors used to trim leaves must be handled point-down and stored blade-inward. No learner should stand on furniture to adjust light sources. Teacher confirms all setups before learners leave the room.

LESSONS.overview: Groups of 4–5 learners each investigate one factor affecting transpiration using freshly cut leafy stems (succulent cuttings such as sweet potato or bean, mirroring the polythene-bag phenomenon). Group A covers leaf undersurfaces with petroleum jelly (reducing functional stomata). Group B directs a fan at their shoot (increasing wind speed). Group C encloses their shoot in a sealed clear polythene bag (raising humidity). Group D varies light intensity by moving the setup from full Kisumu afternoon sunlight to shade. All groups state a hypothesis, identify variables, measure initial stem mass or initial water volume in the beaker, and sketch their setup. Safety rules are reviewed before any equipment is touched. The lesson closes with each group posting their hypothesis and variable table on the Driving Question Board.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners individually write a prediction in their science journals answering: 'Your group will change ONE thing about the environment or the leaf surface of a freshly cut sweet-potato shoot. Before you touch any equipment, predict — will your change make the plant lose water FASTER, SLOWER, or the SAME? Write one sentence explaining WHY you think so, using what you know about stomata and the polythene-bag observation from Lesson 3.' After 4 minutes of individual silent writing, pairs share their reasoning for 2 minutes. The teacher then cold-calls six learners (two per factor group) to voice predictions aloud, and the class votes silently (thumbs up/down/sideways) on whether they agree.
framework.teacherMoves:
1. Display the anchoring phenomenon image (polythene bag with condensation droplets and the red-stained xylem cross-section) on the board. Say: 'Look at this bag. Water got out of the plant even though no liquid water was added. Today YOU are going to find out what makes that process faster or slower — but first, predict.' 
2. Issue the prediction prompt on a half-sheet or project it. Allow 4 minutes of SILENT individual writing. Do NOT accept shouted answers during this time. 
3. After 4 minutes say: 'Turn to your partner. You have 90 seconds. Tell them your prediction AND one piece of evidence from our earlier lessons that supports it.' 
4. After partner talk, cold-call SIX learners: 'Amina — what did you predict for Group B, the fan group, and why?' (WAIT 12 seconds for response.) Repeat for five more learners from different groups. 
5. Conduct a silent vote: 'Thumbs up if you agree with Amina's reasoning, sideways if unsure, down if you disagree.' Note distribution on board without affirming or correcting — say: 'We will test these ideas today. Hold your prediction — we will revisit it at the end.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Individual Predict-Then-Share (a variation of Think-Pair-Share anchored to the phenomenon). This activates prior knowledge about stomata and transpiration from Lessons 3–4, surfaces existing misconceptions (e.g., 'petroleum jelly blocks ALL water loss'), and creates cognitive dissonance that motivates careful experimental design. Recording the prediction in writing externalises thinking so learners can compare it to results in Lesson 6.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher circulates during silent writing and reads over shoulders. Observable indicators of understanding: learner mentions stomata, water vapour, or evaporation in their prediction rationale. Red flag: learner predicts with no mechanistic reason (e.g., 'it will be faster because of the fan' with no link to evaporation rate or stomata). Teacher notes 2–3 such learners by name for targeted questioning during Phase 3.

framework.learnerExperience:
Groups move to their pre-labelled bench stations. Each station has: a freshly cut leafy stem (sweet potato or bean cutting, approximately 15 cm, cut under water to prevent air embolism), a 250 ml beaker of water with a thin layer of cooking oil on top (to reduce evaporation from the water surface — a controlled variable), a balance or measuring cylinder for initial mass/volume, and group-specific equipment. 
• Group A (Petroleum Jelly): Learners use a cotton bud to coat the UNDER surface of every leaf on their stem with petroleum jelly, then place the stem in their beaker. They record the number of leaves coated and the initial water volume. 
• Group B (Wind / Fan): Learners set up their stem in the beaker at a fixed distance (30 cm) from a small table fan. Fan is switched on at the lowest setting. They record initial water volume and air temperature at the fan outlet using a thermometer. 
• Group C (Humidity / Polythene Bag): Learners place a clear polythene bag loosely over the shoot (NOT the beaker) and seal it at the stem with a rubber band, leaving the stem in water. They record initial water volume and note starting bag clarity. 
• Group D (Light Intensity): Learners position one setup in direct afternoon sunlight near the window and one in the shade of the corridor, recording initial water volume and light intensity category (full sun / shade). 
All groups fill in a pre-printed variable table (Independent Variable / Dependent Variable / Controlled Variables) and write their hypothesis in the format: 'If [independent variable changes], then [dependent variable] will [increase/decrease/stay the same] because [mechanistic reason].' Groups sketch their apparatus setup with labels.
framework.teacherMoves:
1. Before any group touches equipment, call the class to attention: 'FREEZE. Before we set up, let us agree on THREE non-negotiables for today.' Read aloud: (a) Petroleum jelly stays on leaves only — not on skin or eyes; wash hands immediately after application. (b) The fan cable must NOT be near the water beakers. (c) Polythene bags are NEVER placed over anyone's face or head. Ask: 'Who can tell me why these rules connect to our experiment's validity as well as our safety?' Cold-call TWO learners. (WAIT 10 seconds each.) 
2. Distribute equipment to bench captains only. Say: 'Bench captain, do NOT distribute until your group has agreed on who does each role: one measurer, one recorder, one apparatus handler, one safety monitor.' Allow 2 minutes for role assignment. 
3. Circulate every 4–5 minutes. At each group, ask ONE probing question: 
   — Group A: 'Why are you coating the UNDER surface and not the top? What do you remember about where stomata are most concentrated?' (WAIT 12 seconds.) 
   — Group B: 'What are you keeping the same between your setup and Group A's setup so we can compare results next lesson?' (WAIT 12 seconds.) 
   — Group C: 'What do you think will happen to the air inside the bag as time goes on? How might that slow transpiration?' (WAIT 15 seconds.) 
   — Group D: 'How will you make sure the stems are otherwise identical — same number of leaves, same stem length?' (WAIT 12 seconds.) 
4. At the 20-minute mark, call a 2-minute whole-class pause: 'Pens down. Each group safety monitor — stand up and check: is any cable near water? Is petroleum jelly off hands? Thumbs up when clear.' Wait for all thumbs before continuing. 
5. At the 28-minute mark: 'Record your INITIAL measurement NOW. You have 90 seconds. This is your Time = 0 data point. Without it, you have no experiment.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured Experimental Design Protocol with Phenomenon Anchoring. Before recording any data, each group must complete the variable table and write a hypothesis in the IF-THEN-BECAUSE format. This structure (adapted from NGSS SEP: Planning and Carrying Out Investigations) prevents learners from 'just following steps' and forces them to articulate the mechanistic link between their manipulated factor and the transpiration rate — directly connecting to the driving question about what happens to the water that travels up through xylem.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher collects the variable tables from each group at the end of this phase (or photographs them with a phone). Observable indicators: (1) Independent variable is correctly identified as the ONE factor the group is changing. (2) Dependent variable is stated as a measurable quantity (water volume lost / mass change), not a vague term like 'transpiration amount'. (3) At least three controlled variables are listed (e.g., same species, same stem length, same number of leaves, same time period, same starting water volume). Red flag: group lists the factor they are changing as BOTH independent AND controlled variable, or lists 'transpiration' as both IV and DV. Teacher addresses this immediately before the group leaves setup.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups rotate to a Gallery Walk of the four bench setups (2 minutes per station). At each station a card shows the group's hypothesis and variable table (posted by the bench captain). Learners use sticky notes to leave one 'I notice…' comment and one 'I wonder…' question on each card. After the gallery walk, the class reconvenes. The teacher selects four 'I wonder' questions (one per group) that best connect to the driving question and asks the originating group to respond. Learners then update their own group's variable table if they received a useful challenge on their sticky notes. Finally, each learner individually answers in their journal: 'Explain, in two sentences, how your group's experiment will give us evidence about what happens to the water that travels up through xylem in the maize plant on our Kisumu farm.'
framework.teacherMoves:
1. Instruct gallery walk: 'You have 8 minutes total — 2 minutes per station. Read the hypothesis and variable table. Leave ONE sticky note starting with 'I notice…' and ONE starting with 'I wonder…'. Be specific — write the group letter on your note.' Use a timer visible to all. 
2. After the gallery walk, say: 'I am going to read four 'I wonder' questions — one about each group's setup. The group whose setup it is will respond. You have 30 seconds to confer with your group before answering.' Read the selected questions one at a time. After each group confers, cold-call the RECORDER (not the bench captain) to answer. (WAIT 12 seconds after question is read before starting group confer time.) 
3. After responses, prompt: 'Did any sticky note on YOUR station make you want to change your variable table? You have 90 seconds to update it if needed.' 
4. Direct individual journal writing: 'On your own — two sentences only — connect YOUR experiment to the maize plant and our driving question. Start with: The water that travels up through xylem in a Kisumu maize plant eventually…' Allow 3 minutes. 
5. Cold-call THREE learners to read their sentences. After each, ask the class: 'Does this sentence use evidence from our lessons, or is it just a claim?' (WAIT 10 seconds for hands before selecting a responder.)
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Gallery Walk with Sticky-Note Critique followed by Phenomenon Re-anchoring Prompt. The gallery walk uses peer-generated questions to stress-test each group's experimental design before any data is collected — a lower-stakes form of peer review that mirrors scientific practice. The individual journal sentence forces each learner to personally connect their small-group experiment back to the whole-plant, whole-farm level of the driving question, preventing the common error of treating transpiration as an isolated lab activity rather than as the endpoint of the water-transport pathway they have been tracing since Lesson 1.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher reads the individual journal sentences while circulating during writing (3 minutes is sufficient to scan 30 sentences). Observable indicator of meeting expectations: sentence names transpiration as water leaving via stomata AND links it to the xylem-transport pathway studied in Lessons 2–4. Red flag: sentence describes transpiration as 'water dripping off leaves' or does not mention stomata or vapour — teacher flags these learners for a brief clarifying conversation before Lesson 6.

framework.learnerExperience: Each group receives two DQB cards: one ORANGE card on which they write their hypothesis ('We think [factor] will [increase/decrease] transpiration because…') and one BLUE card on which they write their biggest remaining question about their experiment or about transpiration in general. Groups post both cards on the class DQB under the column header 'What we are testing — Lesson 5.' The class then does a 3-minute silent read of all posted cards. Learners place a small dot sticker on the ONE blue question they most want answered by Lesson 6. The teacher records the top-voted question on a separate 'priority question' strip at the top of the DQB.
framework.teacherMoves:
1. Distribute orange and blue cards. Say: 'Orange card: your group's hypothesis — write it in the IF-THEN-BECAUSE format, exactly as it appears on your variable table. Blue card: the one thing you most need to know to interpret your results next lesson. You have 3 minutes.' 
2. Groups post cards simultaneously. Say: 'Bench captains, post your cards now. Stick them under Lesson 5 — hypotheses on the left, questions on the right.' 
3. Direct silent read: 'Stand up, walk to the DQB, read ALL eight cards in silence. You have 3 minutes. No talking.' 
4. Distribute dot stickers (one per learner): 'Put your dot on the ONE blue question that YOU most want us to answer in Lesson 6. One dot only.' 
5. Tally dots. Read the winning question aloud. Say: 'This becomes our priority question for Lesson 6. Write it at the top of your journal page for next lesson.' 
6. Gesture to the full DQB and say: 'Look at how our board has grown. In Lesson 1 we asked why red dye only went through certain channels. Today we are testing four different ways that water leaves the plant at the other end of that same journey. Our driving question is getting closer to a full answer — but we need data first.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Hypothesis Posting and Democratic Prioritisation on the DQB. Making hypotheses public creates accountability — groups know their prediction will be compared to real data in Lesson 6. The dot-voting ritual gives learners agency over the inquiry direction and models how scientific communities prioritise research questions. Connecting the DQB growth to the original phenomenon (red-dye channels → transpiration endpoint) keeps the storyline coherent across the 8-lesson sequence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher photographs the full DQB after posting. Observable indicators: orange cards use IF-THEN-BECAUSE format; the named independent variable matches the group's assigned factor; blue question cards are mechanistic (e.g., 'Will the bag eventually become so humid that transpiration stops completely?') rather than procedural (e.g., 'How long do we wait?'). Red flag: a group's orange card states a hypothesis that is not falsifiable by their experimental setup — teacher returns the card with a prompt: 'How will you measure this with the equipment at your station?'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners individually update the cumulative plant-transport model they have been building since Lesson 1. Today's addition: on their model diagram of a maize plant, each learner draws and labels the STOMATA on the leaf surface and adds arrows showing water vapour leaving through the stomata. They add a second annotation layer showing their group's factor — e.g., Group A draws petroleum jelly blocking stomata pores; Group B draws wind arrows accelerating vapour removal; Group C draws humidity arrows slowing vapour gradient; Group D draws a sun/shade symbol affecting stomata opening. Learners write one sentence under their model: 'My group's experiment will change the rate of transpiration by changing _____, which affects _____ in the stomata/environment.'
framework.teacherMoves:
1. Say: 'Open your cumulative model — the diagram we have been adding to since Lesson 1. Today you add the transpiration endpoint. First, everyone draws stomata on the leaf surface — small pores on the underside. Add arrows showing water vapour leaving. You have 2 minutes.' (WAIT and circulate. Remind learners: 'Stomata are mostly on the LOWER epidermis — check your notes from Lesson 3.') 
2. After 2 minutes: 'Now add YOUR group's factor to the model. Show HOW it changes transpiration using arrows, symbols, or a small diagram. You have 3 minutes.' 
3. Cold-call ONE learner from each of the four groups to hold up and briefly explain their model addition (30 seconds each): 'Otieno — show us where you drew the petroleum jelly and explain what it does to the water vapour.' (WAIT 10 seconds.) Repeat for Groups B, C, D. 
4. Say: 'Write your one-sentence annotation now. It must name your independent variable AND name the mechanism — stomata, evaporation gradient, or stomata aperture.' Allow 2 minutes. 
5. Close: 'In Lesson 6, we collect our data. In Lesson 7, we use data from ALL four groups to build a complete explanation. Keep your model safe — you will need it.' Point to the driving question on the wall: 'We started by asking where water goes after it reaches the topmost leaves of a Kisumu maize plant. Today you designed experiments to find out. Next lesson — the evidence.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision (individual, annotated diagram). The model has served as a running record of the class's growing understanding since Lesson 1 (xylem pathway → osmosis → translocation → transpiration). Adding the factor-specific annotation today ensures each learner personally represents the mechanistic link between their experiment and the broader transport pathway — preventing compartmentalised thinking where 'the experiment' and 'the model' are treated as separate activities. Sharing model additions via cold-call creates a rapid whole-class synthesis of all four experimental factors.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher collects models for a 5-minute review between lessons (or photographs them). Observable indicators: stomata are drawn on the LOWER leaf surface (not upper); water vapour arrows exit through stomata (not through the leaf blade generally); the group-specific factor is mechanistically represented (e.g., Group A shows blocked pores, not just a label 'petroleum jelly'). Red flag: learner draws water dripping from leaf edges rather than vapour through stomata — misconception that transpiration is liquid dripping, not vapour diffusion. Teacher prepares a targeted correction prompt for the start of Lesson 6.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect on the following: (1) HYPOTHESIS QUALITY — Did all four groups write hypotheses in the IF-THEN-BECAUSE format with a mechanistic reason, or did groups default to vague predictions? If mechanistic reasoning was weak, plan to open Lesson 6 with a whole-class review of one strong and one weak hypothesis (anonymised) before data collection begins. (2) VARIABLE IDENTIFICATION — Were learners able to distinguish between independent, dependent, and controlled variables, or did any group list their factor as both IV and a controlled variable? This is a high-frequency misconception; if it appeared in more than one group, insert a 5-minute variable-sorting activity at the start of Lesson 6 using a worked example (e.g., 'In an experiment on ugali cooking time, what is the IV if we change flame size?'). (3) SAFETY COMPLIANCE — Were all three non-negotiable safety rules observed throughout? Note any specific incidents for the school safety log and adjust bench layout if water and electrical equipment were too close. (4) DQB ENGAGEMENT — Did the dot-voting produce a genuine priority question, or did learners place dots randomly? If the winning question is procedural rather than conceptual, reframe it as a conceptual question for the start of Lesson 6 and explain to learners why conceptual questions drive science forward. (5) PHENOMENON CONNECTION — When learners wrote their two-sentence journal entries, did they connect their experiment back to the maize plant and the driving question, or did they describe their experiment in isolation? If fewer than 70% of sentences made the connection, dedicate the first 5 minutes of Lesson 6 to re-reading the driving question together and explicitly mapping each group's factor onto the whole-plant diagram.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: A freshly cut sweet-potato or bean stem was placed in a beaker of water. Different groups changed one factor each: Group A coated leaf undersurfaces with petroleum jelly; Group B directed a fan at the shoot; Group C enclosed the shoot in a sealed clear polythene bag; Group D placed their setup in full Kisumu afternoon sunlight versus shade. Each group recorded the initial water volume at Time = 0.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Transpiration — the loss of water vapour from plant surfaces — can be affected by leaf surface conditions (open or blocked stomata), wind speed, surrounding humidity, and light intensity. A fair test requires changing only ONE variable at a time while keeping all others constant. The rate of transpiration is measured by how much water the plant loses over time.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Stomata are small pores, mostly on the underside of leaves, through which water vapour diffuses out of the plant into the surrounding air. The rate of this diffusion depends on the concentration gradient of water vapour between the inside of the leaf and the air outside. Anything that increases that gradient (wind removing vapour, bright light opening stomata wider) speeds transpiration; anything that reduces it (high humidity in a sealed bag, petroleum jelly blocking pores) slows it. This is the final stage of the water journey that began when roots absorbed water from the Kisumu farm soil and xylem carried it to the topmost leaves.
