LESSONS.title: Transpiration Data Collection and Analysis: What Patterns Does Our Evidence Reveal?
LESSONS.aresKeywords: transpiration rate, data collection, bar graph, line graph, humidity, wind speed, light intensity, stomata, water vapour, evidence-based explanation

slo.purpose: Learners collect final transpiration measurements from their group experiments, pool class data, analyse patterns in graphs, and use evidence to explain how environmental factors control the rate of water loss from plant surfaces.
slo.knowledge: Learners will be able to: (1) state how wind speed, humidity, light intensity, and blocked stomata each affect the rate of transpiration; (2) explain the relationship between the stomatal gradient and the direction of water vapour movement; (3) link experimental findings back to the polythene-bag observation from Lesson 1.
slo.skills: Learners will be able to: (1) record transpiration measurements accurately in a data table; (2) construct and interpret bar graphs and line graphs from class-pooled data; (3) identify patterns and anomalies in data sets; (4) use evidence to support or refute their earlier hypotheses.
slo.attitudes: Learners demonstrate scientific integrity by recording actual results even when they differ from their hypothesis; they show collaborative respect when pooling and comparing group data.
slo.keyInquiry: Why is transport in plants important? — This lesson advances the answer by showing that transpiration is not random: its rate is controlled by measurable environmental conditions, which in turn affects how efficiently a maize plant on a Kenyan farm can pull water from the soil to its topmost leaves.
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lesson 5 learners designed and set up transpiration experiments. Lesson 6 is the evidence-collection and analysis lesson: groups read their final measurements, pool data on the class board, draw graphs, and identify patterns. This evidence will feed directly into Lesson 7, where the significance of transpiration for plant survival and Kenyan water cycling will be explained.
slo.safety6otes: Handle plants and measuring equipment gently. Wash hands after handling petroleum jelly or any plant material. Ensure fans used in the wind experiment are placed on stable surfaces and kept away from water. No direct eye contact with bright lamps used in the light-intensity experiment.

LESSONS.overview: Groups collect their final water-loss measurements from the Lesson 5 set-ups, enter data into a class table on the board, and draw graphs. Through guided sensemaking the class identifies which factor caused the greatest increase or decrease in transpiration rate and explains the mechanism behind each pattern. The lesson closes by reconnecting to both the polythene-bag phenomenon and the driving question, and learners update their evidence on the Driving Question Board.

framework.learnerExperience: Before reading their final measurements, each learner individually writes two sentences in their science notebook: (1) a ranked prediction of which experimental group they expect showed the HIGHEST transpiration rate and why, and (2) a ranked prediction of which group showed the LOWEST rate. Learners refer to the hypothesis they wrote in Lesson 5 and circle whether they still agree with it or have changed their mind based on what they have observed qualitatively over the experiment period. Pairs briefly share their rankings with each other (1 minute).
framework.teacherMoves: Teacher opens with a brief recap hook: 'Cast your mind back to Lesson 1 — we saw water droplets collecting inside a polythene bag sealed around a leafy branch in the afternoon sun here in Kisumu. Today we finally have the numbers to explain EXACTLY why that happened and what controls how fast it happens.' Teacher then says: 'Before we read a single number, I want you to make one last prediction. In your notebook, rank the four experimental conditions — blocked stomata, high wind, high humidity, and bright light — from the one you expect lost the MOST water to the one that lost the LEAST. Write your reason in one sentence.' Allow 90 seconds of silent individual thinking. Teacher circulates and notes two or three contrasting predictions to revisit after data collection.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction-before-data routine creates cognitive commitment so that learners experience the productive tension of comparing prediction to evidence — a core scientific practice. Recalling the polythene-bag phenomenon re-anchors the lesson in the real-world context.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher scans notebooks during circulation to check whether learners are using mechanistic reasoning (e.g., referencing stomata, concentration gradient, or water vapour) rather than purely intuitive ranking. This informs the depth of prompting needed during the Explain phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Step 1 — Final Measurements (8 minutes): Each group carefully reads and records the final mass (or water level, depending on their set-up) of their potometer or sealed-bag apparatus. They subtract the initial measurement recorded in Lesson 5 to calculate water lost in grams or millilitres. They also note qualitative observations: Did leaves wilt? Did condensation form? Was there visible change in soil moisture? They enter all values into their group data table using the template provided in Lesson 5. Step 2 — Class Data Pool (4 minutes): One representative from each group writes their group result on the class data table drawn on the board. The table has five columns: Experimental condition | Initial mass (g) | Final mass (g) | Water lost (g) | Rate (g per 10 min). Teacher or a nominated learner completes the rate column together as a class by dividing water lost by the number of 10-minute intervals the experiment ran. Step 3 — Graph Construction (6 minutes): Each learner individually draws either a bar graph (comparing the four conditions) or a line graph (if the light-intensity group has multiple data points at different lux levels) in their notebook. Axes must be labelled with units. Learners use the class-pooled data so that every individual has the full picture.
framework.teacherMoves: During Step 1, teacher moves from group to group asking: 'Has the result surprised you? How does it compare to your Lesson 5 hypothesis?' [WAIT TIME: after each question, pause for 10 seconds before prompting further.] During Step 2, teacher reads aloud each group result as it goes on the board and asks the class: 'Does anyone want to question this number before we accept it into our class table? Could it be an outlier?' This models scientific peer review in a low-stakes way. During Step 3, teacher demonstrates on the board how to choose the correct graph type: 'We use a bar graph when our independent variable is CATEGORICAL — like type of condition. We use a line graph when it is CONTINUOUS — like light intensity measured in lux. Which applies to your group?' [WAIT TIME: 15 seconds for learners to decide before teacher confirms.]
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Pooling data across groups creates a richer evidence base than any single group could generate — mirroring how scientists share findings. Drawing graphs by hand reinforces the link between numbers and visual patterns.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher checks that axes are correctly labelled with units and that the dependent variable (water lost in g or rate in g per 10 min) is always on the y-axis. Common error to watch for: learners plotting initial mass rather than change in mass.

framework.learnerExperience: Step 1 — Pattern Identification (4 minutes): Using their completed graphs, learners answer three analysis questions in their notebooks: (Q1) Which condition produced the highest transpiration rate? (Q2) Which condition produced the lowest rate? (Q3) Describe the trend — as wind speed increases / as humidity increases / as light increases, what happens to the rate? Each group is assigned the question most relevant to their experiment. Step 2 — Mechanism Discussion (5 minutes): Groups discuss the MECHANISM behind their pattern using a sentence stem on the board: 'The rate of transpiration was [higher/lower] under [condition] because [stomata / concentration gradient / water vapour / diffusion / guard cells]...' A representative from each group shares their sentence with the class. Teacher facilitates by linking all explanations back to the water vapour concentration gradient between leaf air spaces and the surrounding air — the single unifying mechanism. Step 3 — Reconnecting to the Phenomenon (3 minutes): Teacher directs attention to a photograph or sketch of the polythene-bag observation from Lesson 1 posted on the wall. Teacher asks: 'The bag was sealed — so why did water droplets still form inside? Use your data as evidence.' Learners write a two-sentence explanation in their notebooks.
framework.teacherMoves: For Q3 pattern analysis, teacher prompts: 'Do not just say the rate went up — tell me WHY by thinking about what is happening at the stomata.' [WAIT TIME: 20 seconds.] During mechanism sharing, if a group says wind increases transpiration, teacher asks the class: 'What exactly does wind DO at the leaf surface that changes the gradient? Turn and tell your partner.' [WAIT TIME: 15 seconds for paired discussion before cold-calling.] For the polythene-bag reconnection, teacher says: 'The bag was sealed and no liquid water was added. Where did the water vapour come from? Your data from the sealed-bag group might help you answer that.' Teacher avoids giving the answer immediately — instead writes on the board: 'Source of water vapour = ?' and lets learners fill it in. Key vocabulary to reinforce orally and in writing: transpiration pull, concentration gradient, stomata, water vapour, diffusion, guard cells. Teacher uses local context: 'Think about a maize field in Siaya County on a hot, windy afternoon after a dry spell — based on our data, what is happening to the water that farmer Atieno irrigated that morning?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: The sentence-stem strategy scaffolds mechanistic explanation without removing cognitive challenge. Reconnecting to the Lesson 1 polythene-bag phenomenon creates a satisfying closure loop — learners see that they now have evidence-based answers to a question that was puzzling in Lesson 1. Local Kenyan agricultural context makes the science personally meaningful.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher collects the two-sentence polythene-bag explanation as an exit-quality check. Look for: (a) learner identifies the leaf as the source of water vapour, (b) learner uses the word stomata or diffusion, (c) learner links the bag sealing to the rise in humidity reducing the gradient. Learners who cannot meet criteria (a) or (b) will need targeted support in Lesson 7.

framework.learnerExperience: Each group receives two sticky notes of different colours. On the FIRST note (green), they write one question from the DQB that their experimental data has now answered — and they write the evidence-based answer in one sentence. On the SECOND note (orange), they write one NEW question their data raised that is still unanswered. Groups take turns posting their notes on the DQB. The teacher reads aloud the answered questions and asks the class to vote by show of hands whether they agree the question is now sufficiently answered. Unanswered questions are flagged for Lesson 7.
framework.teacherMoves: Teacher says: 'Scientists do not just collect data and put it away — they ask what their data means for the next question. Look at our DQB from Lesson 1. Point to one question that our graphs today can now answer.' After groups post, teacher facilitates a brief gallery walk (1 minute, standing at desks and looking at the board) then says: 'I can see several groups have asked WHY transpiration matters if it means the plant is losing water — that is EXACTLY what Lesson 7 will tackle. Hold that question.' Teacher uses a contrasting-cases move: 'Group A says high wind INCREASES water loss. Group C says high humidity DECREASES it. How can BOTH be true at the same time — what is the variable they are both affecting?' [WAIT TIME: 20 seconds before accepting responses.]
framework.sensemakingStrategy: The two-colour sticky note protocol makes the distinction between answered and open questions visible and concrete. The contrasting-cases prompt (wind vs. humidity) deepens understanding by showing that both variables act on the same underlying mechanism — the concentration gradient.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher scans the answered-question notes for quality of evidence citation. A strong note will reference a specific measurement (e.g., 'the sealed-bag group lost only 0.3 g versus 1.8 g in the open group, so humidity reduces transpiration by narrowing the concentration gradient'). Vague notes are verbally prompted: 'Can you add a number from our class table to support that?'

framework.learnerExperience: In the final 4 minutes, each learner adds a NEW layer to the running annotated diagram they began building in earlier lessons. Using a coloured pen different from previous lessons, they annotate the leaf region of their diagram to show: (1) an open stoma with an arrow indicating the direction of water vapour movement; (2) a label showing the high-concentration water vapour region inside the leaf air space and the lower-concentration region outside; (3) a note showing how wind, humidity, and light each affect this gradient, with a plus or minus symbol to indicate whether each factor increases or decreases the rate. Learners who finish early add a note connecting transpiration rate back to the speed at which water is pulled up the xylem from the roots — previewing the cohesion-tension content of Lesson 7.
framework.teacherMoves: Teacher circulates and prompts: 'Show me on your diagram where the concentration gradient exists — draw a dotted line between the two regions.' [WAIT TIME: 10 seconds.] For extension learners, teacher asks: 'If transpiration rate increases on a hot Kisumu afternoon, what does that mean for the rate at which water and dissolved mineral salts are moving up the xylem of a maize stem? Add an arrow to show that link.' Teacher closes the lesson with a forward-bridge statement: 'Today you have proved with real measurements that environmental conditions control how fast water leaves a plant. In Lesson 7 we will ask — is transpiration a problem for the plant, or is it actually essential? And we will explore what farmers around the Mau Forest need to know about this.' Teacher thanks learners for scientific integrity in recording honest results even when they differed from predictions.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Incremental model building across lessons creates a cumulative, visible knowledge artifact. Using a different colour for each lesson update makes the progression of understanding tangible and helps learners see how each lesson adds a new explanatory layer.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher checks that the concentration gradient is correctly drawn — high inside the leaf, lower outside. Common misconception to catch: learners who draw the arrow pointing INTO the leaf, suggesting water vapour enters rather than leaves. This is corrected in real time by asking: 'Which side has more water vapour — the air space inside the leaf or the dry air outside on a sunny Kisumu afternoon?'

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: (1) Did all four experimental groups obtain plausible data, or did any set-up fail to show a measurable difference? If so, why — and how will you address this in Lesson 7 discussion? (2) Were learners able to articulate the concentration gradient mechanism in their own words, or did they rely only on memorised phrases? (3) Did the polythene-bag reconnection feel natural, or did learners still seem puzzled? Plan a brief revision of diffusion and water vapour for the opening of Lesson 7 if needed. (4) Note which learners posted strong evidence-cited sticky notes on the DQB — these learners can serve as peer explainers in Lesson 7 group work. (5) Consider whether the graph-drawing time was sufficient — if many learners did not finish, allow 5 minutes at the start of Lesson 7 for completion before moving to significance discussion.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that the group with high wind lost the most water, the group with blocked stomata (petroleum jelly) lost the least, the group in the sealed polythene bag lost very little, and the group under bright light lost more than the group in shade. We pooled all four group results into one class data table and drew bar graphs showing these differences.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that the rate of transpiration is controlled by the concentration gradient of water vapour between the inside of a leaf and the surrounding air. Wind increases the rate by sweeping away water vapour outside the stomata, restoring a steep gradient. High humidity reduces the rate by raising the water vapour concentration outside, flattening the gradient. Bright light increases the rate by causing stomata to open wider. Blocking stomata reduces the rate almost to zero.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We explained why water droplets formed inside the sealed polythene bag in Lesson 1: the leaf was continuously losing water vapour through its stomata by diffusion down the concentration gradient, and when the bag trapped that vapour it condensed on the cool inner surface. This shows that transpiration is a continuous, measurable process driven by physical gradients — not a random event — and its rate changes predictably when environmental conditions change.

LESSONS.title: Importance of Transpiration and Community Application

slo.purpose: To explain the significance of transpiration in plant life and communicate its importance to the community through a farmer-focused awareness message.
slo.knowledge: Learners will be able to: (i) describe the significance of transpiration — cooling of leaves, generation of transpiration pull (cohesion-tension theory), and distribution of mineral salts; (ii) explain the role of transpiration in local and regional water cycling, with reference to the Mau Forest catchment; (iii) explain the importance of proper watering, manuring, and responsible fertiliser use (DAP, CAN, Urea) for sustaining crop growth.
slo.skills: Constructing explanations that link cohesion-tension theory to the upward movement of water observed in the red-dye phenomenon; obtaining, evaluating, and communicating information through drafting a community awareness message for farmers.
slo.attitudes: Learners appreciate the role of transport in plants and show patriotism by sensitising the community on the importance of watering and manuring plants to sustain plant growth, and by creating awareness on the responsible use of fertilisers (Di-ammonium Phosphate, Calcium Ammonium Nitrate, Urea) in boosting crop production.
slo.keyInquiry: Why is transport in plants important?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lessons 1–6 learners gathered evidence — the red-dye maize stem showed water travelling upward through xylem, while the polythene-bag experiment revealed water vapour escaping from leaves. Lesson 7 now asks: WHY does the plant lose water through transpiration at all? Learners synthesise all prior evidence to explain the three key functions of transpiration (cooling, transpiration pull, mineral distribution), connect those functions to the Mau Forest water cycle, and translate their understanding into a practical community message for farmers in the Kisumu region — directly advancing the driving question by accounting for what ultimately happens to the water after it reaches the topmost leaves.
slo.safetyNotes: No hazardous chemicals are used in this lesson. If printed fertiliser packets (DAP, CAN, Urea) are brought in as realia, learners must not open the packets; hands should be washed after handling. Ensure learners are seated safely during whole-class and group discussion phases. Supervise use of any digital devices according to school ICT policy.

LESSONS.overview: Lesson 7 is the EXPLAIN lesson in the 8-lesson sequence on Transport in Plants. Building on the red-dye maize stem evidence (xylem channels) and the polythene-bag transpiration evidence from earlier lessons, learners now synthesise WHY transpiration occurs and why it matters — for the individual maize plant, for Kenyan farms, and for the wider environment including the Mau Forest catchment. The lesson opens with a brief predict-and-recall warm-up, moves through a teacher-facilitated whole-class discussion to construct explanations for the three functions of transpiration, then shifts to small-group work where learners research and discuss the environmental importance of transpiration in local water cycling. The lesson culminates in a community action task: each group drafts a short Swahili/English awareness message for farmers on proper watering, manuring, and responsible use of DAP, CAN, and Urea fertilisers. The Driving Question Board is revisited and updated. SEPs foregrounded: Constructing Explanations; Obtaining, Evaluating, and Communicating Information.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners individually write a 2-minute 'exit prediction' in their notebooks: 'The maize plant keeps losing water through its leaves even on a hot afternoon in Kisumu. Give TWO reasons why you think this water loss might actually be USEFUL to the plant — not just wasteful.' They then share predictions with a shoulder partner before a whole-class share-out.
framework.teacherMoves: 1. Display the anchoring phenomenon images side-by-side on the board or screen: (A) the cross-section of the red-dye maize stem showing vivid red rings in the xylem, and (B) the polythene bag with water droplets on its inner surface. Say: 'Look at these two images we have been investigating all week. Image A shows us HOW water travels up — through the xylem. Image B shows us that water eventually LEAVES the plant through the leaves. Today's big question is: WHY does the plant allow this water to escape? Is it a mistake — or is it useful?' (WAIT 10 seconds for silent individual thinking.) 2. Give the written prediction task. Allow 2 minutes of silent individual writing. 3. Cold-call 4 learners (select: 1 high-confidence, 1 mid-confidence, 2 learners who rarely volunteer — use the class register to track). Record their predictions verbatim on the board in two columns: 'Water loss is useful because…' | 'Water loss might be harmful because…'. Do NOT evaluate — say: 'We are not judging yet — we are collecting ideas to test against evidence today.' 4. Leave predictions visible for the entire lesson so learners can revisit them.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Elicit-Before-Explain (predict-first protocol): by articulating prior ideas before instruction, learners create a cognitive 'hook' for new information. The side-by-side phenomenon images maintain the storyline thread and prime learners to think causally (not just descriptively) about transpiration.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Every learner has at least one written prediction in their notebook within 2 minutes. Teacher scans notebooks during the cold-call phase. If fewer than half the class can generate any prediction, pause and ask a scaffold question: 'Think about what happens to YOUR body when you sweat on a hot day in Nairobi — does sweating help you or hurt you?' This connects to prior knowledge from respiration and homeostasis contexts.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in groups of 4–5. Each group receives a Resource Pack containing: (i) a printed summary data table from Lessons 4–5 showing how stomata count, wind, temperature, and humidity affected transpiration rates in the potometer experiments; (ii) a short illustrated text (one A4 page, bilingual Swahili/English) on the cohesion-tension theory, the cooling function of transpiration, and mineral salt distribution; (iii) a printed excerpt or teacher-summarised paragraph on the role of forests in water cycling, specifically referencing the Mau Forest catchment in the Rift Valley and Lake Victoria's water balance. Groups read, discuss, and annotate: they underline key evidence that answers 'Why is transpiration useful?' and circle anything that surprises or confuses them. Groups also examine the fertiliser packet labels (DAP, CAN, Urea) brought as realia (sealed; not opened) and identify which nutrients each provides to the maize plant.
framework.teacherMoves: 1. Before distributing packs, say: 'In the last six lessons you gathered evidence. Now we are going to use that evidence plus new information to BUILD an explanation — like a scientist does. Scientists do not just collect data; they explain WHY the data means what it means.' 2. Distribute Resource Packs. Give groups exactly 10 minutes to read and annotate. Set a visible timer. Circulate — spend no more than 2 minutes per group. Prompt with: 'What does the cohesion-tension theory tell us about WHY the red rings appeared only in the xylem?' (WAIT 12 seconds before offering a hint.) 3. At the 5-minute mark, call out: 'Make sure your group has identified at least THREE pieces of evidence from our earlier experiments that connect to transpiration being useful.' 4. At 10 minutes, call time. Ask each group to appoint a 'reporter' for the next phase. 5. Hold up the sealed DAP, CAN, and Urea packets. Ask: 'Before I tell you what these are — what do you already know about how farmers in the Rift Valley use these white powders on their maize?' Cold-call 3 learners. Record responses. Then confirm: 'These are fertilisers. DAP gives nitrogen and phosphorus; CAN gives calcium and nitrogen; Urea gives nitrogen. Today we will connect these to what the xylem and phloem do inside the maize plant.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Evidence-Based Discussion with Annotated Text: learners physically mark text (underline/circle) to distinguish evidence from explanation and to flag confusion. This is a disciplinary literacy strategy (SEP: Obtaining, Evaluating, and Communicating Information) that makes the evidence-to-explanation move visible. Connecting fertiliser realia to xylem/phloem transport maintains the phenomenon storyline and grounds the chemistry in the biology.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: each group's annotated resource pack shows at least 3 underlines (useful functions) and at least 1 circle (surprise/confusion). Teacher uses circled items as discussion seeds in Phase 3. If a group has no circles, prompt: 'Does everything here make complete sense to you? What would you want to ask a Kenyan botanist if she walked in right now?'

framework.learnerExperience: Groups share their findings in a structured whole-class discussion. The teacher co-constructs a 'Transpiration Functions Wall' on the board — three columns: (1) Cooling of Leaves, (2) Transpiration Pull / Cohesion-Tension, (3) Mineral Salt Distribution. Learners contribute evidence and explanations; the teacher scribes, questions, and refines. Learners then individually write a 3-sentence 'scientist's explanation' in their notebooks linking the phenomenon (red dye in xylem; water droplets in the bag) to at least TWO functions of transpiration. A second mini-discussion explores the Mau Forest connection: how transpiration from millions of trees feeds water back into the atmosphere and sustains rainfall patterns across western Kenya and the Lake Victoria basin.
framework.teacherMoves: 1. Draw the three-column 'Transpiration Functions Wall' on the board. Say: 'We are going to BUILD this wall together using YOUR evidence and the new reading. Each brick in this wall must be supported by evidence — not just opinion.' 2. Column 1 — Cooling: Ask reporter from Group 1: 'What did your reading say about why a maize leaf does not overheat on a hot afternoon in Kisumu?' After response, ask the class: 'Do you AGREE or can you add evidence? Think back to our potometer results — what happened to transpiration rate when temperature was high?' (WAIT 15 seconds.) Cold-call 2 more learners. Scribe key phrase: 'Evaporation of water from stomata absorbs latent heat → cools the leaf.' 3. Column 2 — Transpiration Pull: Ask reporter from Group 2: 'How does the cohesion-tension theory explain the RED RINGS we saw in the maize stem?' (WAIT 12 seconds.) If response is incomplete, scaffold: 'Water molecules hold onto each other — what is that called? And they hold onto the xylem wall — what is that called?' Build the explanation: 'Transpiration at the leaf surface → creates tension (negative pressure) → pulls the water column upward through xylem → this is the transpiration pull.' Point to the red-dye image: 'THIS is why the dye moved up. Without transpiration — no pull. Without the pull — the water stays in the beaker.' 4. Column 3 — Mineral Salt Distribution: Ask: 'DAP contains phosphorus and nitrogen. Once a farmer in the Rift Valley applies DAP around a maize plant, HOW does that phosphorus reach the topmost leaf?' (WAIT 15 seconds.) Cold-call 3 learners. Guide toward: 'Minerals dissolved in soil water → absorbed through root hair cells → carried upward in the xylem by the transpiration stream → distributed to all parts of the plant.' Say: 'So transpiration is not just water loss — it is the DELIVERY MECHANISM for mineral nutrients.' 5. Individual writing (3 minutes silent): 'In your own words, write 3 sentences explaining — using evidence from our experiments — why transpiration is important for the maize plant.' 6. Mau Forest mini-discussion (5 minutes): Display a simple sketch map of Kenya showing the Mau Forest, Rift Valley rivers, and Lake Victoria. Say: 'The Mau Forest is Kenya's largest water tower. Millions of trees transpire every day. Where does all that water vapour go?' Cold-call 4 learners. Build toward: 'Water vapour → forms clouds → returns as rainfall → feeds rivers → feeds Lake Victoria → supports farming communities in Kisumu, Kericho, and the broader western Kenya region.' Ask: 'So when forests are cut down — like parts of the Mau — what happens to this cycle?' (WAIT 12 seconds.) Accept 3 responses. Say: 'This is why transpiration matters beyond the single maize plant — it is part of Kenya's water security.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Co-Constructed Concept Wall (collaborative explanation-building): rather than the teacher delivering a lecture, the board serves as a shared artefact that learners contribute to brick-by-brick. This makes explanation-building a social, visible, iterative process (SEP: Constructing Explanations). Anchoring each column back to the phenomenon images (red dye; water droplets in bag) sustains the storyline and prevents abstraction from becoming disconnected from the original observations.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (i) the Transpiration Functions Wall has at least 2 pieces of learner-generated evidence per column by end of discussion; (ii) individual 3-sentence explanations include at least one reference to the phenomenon (red dye OR water droplets) AND at least one named function of transpiration. Teacher collects 6 notebooks (2 high, 2 mid, 2 lower) to scan during the group work in Phase 4. If explanations are purely definitional (no evidence linkage), teacher pauses Phase 4 and models one sentence: 'The red dye moved up through the xylem because transpiration at the leaf pulled the water column upward — this is the transpiration pull (cohesion-tension theory).'

framework.learnerExperience: The class returns to the Driving Question Board displayed at the front of the room. Learners individually write one sticky note (or a strip of paper) answering a specific sub-question of the DQB that this lesson has addressed. They also add at least one NEW question that Lesson 7 has raised for them — especially about what happens when transpiration is disrupted (e.g., drought, deforestation, over-fertilisation). Groups then do a 'gallery walk' past the updated DQB for 3 minutes, reading peers' additions and placing a tick on any idea they agree with or a question mark on anything they want to discuss further.
framework.teacherMoves: 1. Uncover the DQB. Point to the driving question written at the top: 'How does a maize plant in a Kenyan farm move water and nutrients from the soil all the way to its topmost leaves — and what happens to that water in the end?' Say: 'At the start of this unit, this question was a mystery. Look at how many of these smaller questions on our board we can now answer.' 2. Read aloud 3 previously posted learner questions from earlier lessons (choose ones directly addressed today — e.g., 'Why does water keep moving up?'; 'What is the point of losing water from leaves?'; 'How do minerals get to the top of the plant?'). For each, ask: 'Can we answer this now? Who wants to give a one-sentence answer?' Cold-call 1 learner per question. Confirm or refine the answer and mark those questions as 'EXPLAINED ✓' on the board. 3. Distribute sticky notes. Say: 'Write ONE thing you can now explain that you could not explain in Lesson 1. Write it as a full sentence. Then write ONE new question this lesson has opened up for you.' Allow 3 minutes silent writing. 4. Learners post their sticky notes on the DQB. Run the gallery walk (3 minutes). 5. After the gallery walk, ask: 'What is still unexplained on our board about the maize plant and water?' Accept 3 responses. Highlight any that will be addressed in Lesson 8 (final lesson — synthesis and summative assessment preparation). Say: 'These open questions are NOT failures — they are the frontier of your learning. Real scientists in Kenya working on drought-resistant maize varieties at KARI [Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organisation] ask questions just like these every day.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board Revision (tracking cumulative understanding): the DQB functions as a living, public record of the class's growing understanding. Marking questions as 'EXPLAINED ✓' gives learners a concrete, visible sense of intellectual progress and motivates engagement with remaining mysteries. The gallery walk activates peer-to-peer evaluation (SEP: Obtaining, Evaluating, and Communicating Information).
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (i) every learner has posted at least one sticky note with a full explanatory sentence AND one new question; (ii) at least 3 previously posted DQB questions are formally marked 'EXPLAINED ✓' with a class-agreed answer. Teacher photographs the updated DQB for the ARES platform record and to inform Lesson 8 planning. If learners cannot articulate any answered question, this signals that Phase 3 explanation-building was insufficient — teacher notes this for differentiated support in Lesson 8.

framework.learnerExperience: Part A — Model Revision (10 min): Each learner opens their cumulative Transport in Plants model (begun in Lesson 1 and revised each lesson). They add a new annotated layer specifically showing: (i) arrows for the transpiration stream from roots → xylem → leaves → stomata → atmosphere; (ii) a label showing where mineral salts (e.g., nitrogen from CAN, phosphorus from DAP) travel within the xylem stream; (iii) a small cloud symbol above the leaf with a dotted arrow back to the Mau Forest sketch, representing the water cycle link. Learners add a colour-coded key distinguishing water movement (blue), mineral movement (green), and water vapour / transpiration loss (red dashed). Part B — Community Awareness Message (15 min): In their groups, learners draft a short awareness message (maximum 80 words, bilingual Swahili/English) addressed to a smallholder maize farmer in the Kisumu region. The message must: (i) explain in simple terms why watering the maize regularly matters (transpiration pull needs a continuous water column); (ii) advise on manuring to improve soil water retention; (iii) give ONE specific, practical tip on responsible fertiliser use — choosing DAP, CAN, or Urea appropriately and avoiding over-application to prevent soil and water pollution. Groups present their messages to the class in a 60-second 'radio broadcast' style — one learner reads it aloud as if speaking on a community FM radio station.
framework.teacherMoves: 1. Model revision: Say: 'Your model has been growing every lesson. Today you are adding the FINAL missing piece — what happens to the water AFTER it reaches the topmost leaf. Add the transpiration stream, the mineral delivery route, and the link to the water cycle. Use the three colours in your key.' Circulate for 10 minutes. Prompt with: 'Where exactly do the mineral salts enter the xylem? Show me on your model.' (WAIT 10 seconds.) Check that models show minerals entering at the root and travelling upward — not downward. 2. Community message task: Say: 'Scientists do not just understand the world — they communicate that understanding to help their communities. A farmer in Kisumu growing maize to feed her family needs to know what YOU now know about transpiration, water, and fertilisers. You are going to write her a message — short enough to broadcast on a community FM station like Radio Lake Victoria.' Circulate during drafting. Prompt groups: 'Would a farmer who has not studied biology understand the word xylem? How would you say it differently?' Encourage use of Kiswahili terms where helpful (e.g., 'mfumo wa usafirishaji wa maji' — water transport system). 3. Radio broadcast presentations: Each group stands and delivers their 60-second broadcast. After each, ask the class: 'Did this message give the farmer ONE specific action they can take? Thumbs up / thumbs sideways / thumbs down.' Briefly affirm specific actions mentioned and gently redirect any message that is too abstract or too technical. 4. Close by returning to the driving question one final time: 'So — what happens to the water in the end?' Cold-call 3 learners for a complete one-sentence answer. Confirm: 'The water travels up through the xylem, pulled by the transpiration stream driven by evaporation at the leaf surface through stomata — and it returns to the atmosphere as water vapour, completing the water cycle that sustains rainfall across western Kenya.' Say: 'In Lesson 8, we will pull everything together and prepare to show what we know.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision + Community Communication (SEP: Constructing Explanations + Communicating Information): the model revision makes the full transport pathway — from soil water uptake through to atmospheric water vapour — visible in a single annotated diagram, integrating all lesson evidence. The community awareness task is an authentic communication challenge that requires learners to translate disciplinary knowledge into accessible language, deepening their own understanding through the act of explanation (the 'protégé effect'). The radio broadcast format is culturally familiar to Kenyan rural contexts and builds public-speaking confidence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (i) learner models show a continuous, annotated transpiration stream from root to atmosphere, with mineral salt pathway labelled and water cycle link included; (ii) community messages are comprehensible to a non-specialist, include at least one specific actionable tip, and reference at least one fertiliser by name (DAP, CAN, or Urea); (iii) class thumb-voting reveals whether peers judge messages as actionable — teacher uses this as a proxy for clarity of explanation. Teacher collects 4 models (one per ability band) for detailed written feedback before Lesson 8.

LESSONS.teacherReflection:
After the lesson, reflect on the following questions and record brief notes in your ARES journal:
1. EXPLANATION QUALITY: Did learners' 3-sentence individual explanations (Phase 3) include evidence from the phenomenon — or were they purely definitional? If most explanations were definitional, plan a brief 5-minute model explanation at the start of Lesson 8 using the red-dye image explicitly.
2. DQB MOMENTUM: Were learners able to identify at least 3 questions from the DQB that this lesson answered? If not, consider whether the Phase 2 resource texts were pitched at the right reading level for your class in Kisumu. Simplify or pre-read aloud in Lesson 8 if needed.
3. COMMUNITY MESSAGE QUALITY: Did the radio broadcast messages strike a balance between scientific accuracy and accessibility? Note which groups produced the strongest messages and consider sharing these on the ARES platform as exemplars for other schools.
4. EQUITY: Did the same learners dominate whole-class discussion across all phases? Review your cold-call log and ensure you are distributing participation equitably — particularly across gender and across learners with different levels of prior attainment.
5. DRIVING QUESTION PROGRESS: The driving question asks what happens to the water 'in the end.' By the end of Lesson 7, can most learners articulate a complete answer — from soil, through root hair cells, up the xylem via transpiration pull, out through stomata, and back to the atmosphere? If not, Lesson 8 must include a synthesis activity (e.g., annotated poster or flow diagram) to consolidate this full pathway before summative assessment.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: In earlier lessons, learners placed a maize seedling's roots in red-dyed water and observed vivid red rings appearing only in the xylem tissue of a cross-sectioned stem. They also observed water droplets forming on the inside of a sealed polythene bag enclosing a leafy plant cutting placed in afternoon sun — even though no liquid water was added to the bag.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Transpiration serves three critical functions for the maize plant: (1) it cools the leaf surface through evaporation, preventing heat damage on hot Kenyan afternoons; (2) it generates the transpiration pull (cohesion-tension mechanism) that is the primary force driving water upward through the xylem against gravity — explaining why the red dye moved upward through those specific channels; and (3) it drives the continuous transpiration stream that carries dissolved mineral salts (such as nitrogen from CAN/Urea and phosphorus from DAP) from the soil, through the roots, and all the way to the topmost leaves. At the landscape scale, transpiration from forests like the Mau Forest feeds water vapour back into the atmosphere, sustaining rainfall patterns that support farming communities across western Kenya and the Lake Victoria basin.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The water that entered the maize plant through its root hair cells — visible as the red dye moving through the xylem rings — ultimately escapes as water vapour through the stomata of the topmost leaves (the water droplets seen on the inside of the polythene bag). This loss is not waste: it is the engine of the entire transport system. Without transpiration pulling water upward through the cohesion-tension mechanism, mineral nutrients dissolved in the soil water could not be delivered to the growing tissues. Responsible farming practices — regular watering to maintain the water column, manuring to improve soil structure and water retention, and careful use of fertilisers (DAP for phosphorus and nitrogen, CAN and Urea for nitrogen) — directly support this transport system and sustain maize crop yields on Kenyan farms.
